Functional Dependencies and Normalization

A self-contained crash guide for someone who studied ER/EER for A2 and skipped the detailed preparation for A3, followed by every scheduled exercise from Chapters 14 and 15 of Elmasri & Navathe (7th ed.) with a full solution behind the Solution button.

You do not need to redo all of A3

Learn how to read relational tables and keys, then spend most of your time on dependencies, normal forms and decomposition.

How this connects to what you already know

In A2 you decided which entities and relationships exist. A3 turns that design into tables. A4 asks whether those tables repeat facts unnecessarily and how to split them without changing the information they represent.

Already familiarThe new skill
An employee belongs to a department.Write Ssn→Dnumber\text{Ssn}\to\text{Dnumber}Ssn→Dnumber as a functional dependency.
A relationship can have its own attribute, such as Hours.Explain why (Ssn, Pnumber) together determines Hours.
Entities have identifying keys.Derive every candidate key from a set of dependencies.
Separate entities usually become separate tables.Prove that your table decomposition is lossless.

Use this as a problem-solving guide

Read with paper beside you. For each worked problem, stop at the prompt and attempt the next step before reading it. The aim is to calculate closures, identify a violating dependency and justify a decomposition yourself.

Scope. The schedule assigns normalisation to Chapters 14 and 15. The actual A4 paper and lecture slides were not supplied, so this guide follows the scheduled textbook questions; it does not claim to predict the assignment. Exercises tagged ★ Must-do match past end-sem and quiz questions.

Notation. ABABAB means the set {A,B}\{A,B\}{A,B}, not multiplication. X+X^+X+ is the closure of the attributes XXX. F+F^+F+ is the set of all dependencies implied by FFF. An arrow →\to→ means “functionally determines”.

What you can skim tonight. Do not reread all the ER diagram notation, subclasses or union categories. Relational algebra query exercises and SQL syntax are not prerequisites for these normalisation calculations. You do need the meaning of projection and natural join, explained in 4.2. The 4NF/5NF extension (Section 6) is lower priority for this short route: read it after the main methods if time permits, or sooner if your lecturer explicitly stressed higher normal forms.

What is inside

    1  A3 catch-up · Ch. 5, 9

    The relational model, without the backlog

    A relation is a table. A tuple is a row. An attribute is a column. A schema lists the table name and columns; an instance is the data currently in it.

    STUDENT(Sid, Name, Email, DeptNo)DEPARTMENT(DeptNo, DeptName)\begin{aligned}&\textsf{STUDENT}(\text{Sid},\ \text{Name},\ \text{Email},\ \text{DeptNo})\\ &\textsf{DEPARTMENT}(\text{DeptNo},\ \text{DeptName})\end{aligned}​STUDENT(Sid, Name, Email, DeptNo)DEPARTMENT(DeptNo, DeptName)​
    Key vocabulary
    TermWhat it means
    SuperkeyA set of columns that uniquely identifies a row in every legal instance. It may include unnecessary columns.
    Candidate keyA minimal superkey. Removing any column makes it stop being a superkey. “Minimal” does not mean smallest among all keys.
    Primary keyOne chosen candidate key. The other candidate keys still matter for normalisation.
    Composite keyA key containing more than one attribute.
    Foreign keyColumn(s) referencing a candidate key in another table, or the same table. It need not be unique in the referencing table.
    Prime attributeAn attribute belonging to at least one candidate key. Nonprime means it belongs to none.

    A concrete distinction

    Suppose Sid and Email are each unique and mandatory. Candidate keys are {Sid} and {Email}. {Sid, Name} is a superkey but not a candidate key because Sid alone works. Choosing Sid as primary key does not stop Email from being prime.

    DeptNo in STUDENT is a foreign key. Many students can have the same DeptNo. DeptNo therefore does not identify a student, even though it identifies a department in DEPARTMENT.

    Keys are constraints, not observations

    Five students having different names today does not establish Name as a key. It must identify a row in every allowed state of the database.

    Primary-key values cannot be NULL. A foreign key must match the referenced key unless NULL is permitted. For the calculations in this guide, use the textbook’s ordinary relational model with atomic values and no NULL complications.

    Textbook §§5.1–5.2; the ER guide is Topic 3.

    Just enough ER-to-table mapping

    Basic mapping rules (not the full A3 syllabus)
    ER ideaRelational result
    Strong entityMake a table of its simple attributes. Flatten a composite Name into its components. Choose a primary key.
    1:N relationshipPut the 1-side key in the N-side table as a foreign key. Put relationship attributes there too.
    M:N relationshipMake a separate table with both participant keys and the relationship attributes. For an ordinary binary M:N, the pair is the key.
    Multivalued attributeMake a separate table with the owner key and one value per row.
    Weak entityInclude the owner key. The usual key is owner key plus partial key.
    DEPARTMENT(DeptNo‾, DeptName)key: DeptNoSTUDENT(Sid‾, Name, DeptNo)key: SidCOURSE(Cid‾, Title)key: CidENROLMENT(Sid, Cid‾, Grade)key: Sid, Cid\begin{aligned}&\textsf{DEPARTMENT}(\underline{\text{DeptNo}},\ \text{DeptName}) &&\text{key: DeptNo}\\ &\textsf{STUDENT}(\underline{\text{Sid}},\ \text{Name},\ \text{DeptNo}) &&\text{key: Sid}\\ &\textsf{COURSE}(\underline{\text{Cid}},\ \text{Title}) &&\text{key: Cid}\\ &\textsf{ENROLMENT}(\underline{\text{Sid},\ \text{Cid}},\ \text{Grade}) &&\text{key: Sid, Cid}\end{aligned}​DEPARTMENT(DeptNo​, DeptName)STUDENT(Sid​, Name, DeptNo)COURSE(Cid​, Title)ENROLMENT(Sid, Cid​, Grade)​​key: DeptNokey: Sidkey: Cidkey: Sid, Cid​

    STUDENT.DeptNo represents a 1:N department–student relationship. ENROLMENT represents an M:N student–course relationship. Grade belongs to the student–course combination, so Sid alone does not determine it.

    Checkpoint: attempt before reading the answer

    A student has one department and can take many courses. A course has many students. Why should DeptName not be copied into every ENROLMENT row? What is the key of ENROLMENT? Which columns are foreign keys?

    Answer

    DeptName describes a department, so copying it per enrolment repeats a fact and creates inconsistent-update risks. Under these assumptions ENROLMENT has key {Sid, Cid}; Sid references STUDENT and Cid references COURSE. If retakes are tracked, add the offering/attempt identifier to the model and reconsider the key.

    Ready to move on? You should be able to read R(A,B,C)R(A,B,C)R(A,B,C), say what a candidate key is, and explain why the key of an M:N table is often a pair. That is enough A3 background to start A4.

    Textbook §9.1. Basic rules only; not the full A3 syllabus.

    2  Dependencies, closure and keys · Ch. 14.1–14.4, 15.1

    Why normalisation exists

    EMP_DEPT(Ssn, Ename, Dno, Dname, Manager)Ssn→Ename, DnoDno→Dname, Manager\begin{aligned}&\textsf{EMP\_DEPT}(\text{Ssn},\ \text{Ename},\ \text{Dno},\ \text{Dname},\ \text{Manager})\\ &\text{Ssn}\to\text{Ename},\,\text{Dno}\qquad \text{Dno}\to\text{Dname},\,\text{Manager}\end{aligned}​EMP_DEPT(Ssn, Ename, Dno, Dname, Manager)Ssn→Ename,DnoDno→Dname,Manager​
    SsnEnameDnoDnameManager
    101Asha10SalesM1
    102Dev10SalesM1
    103Mira20DesignM2

    The table mixes facts about an employee with facts about a department. Department 10’s name and manager are repeated for every employee in it.

    The three update anomalies
    AnomalyWhat goes wrong
    ModificationRenaming Sales requires changing multiple rows. Missing one row creates conflicting department names.
    InsertionYou cannot represent a new department with no employees in this table without inventing an employee or using a missing employee key.
    DeletionDeleting the last employee in department 20 also deletes the only stored record of its name and manager.

    Separate the kinds of facts

    EMPLOYEE(Ssn‾, Ename, Dno)key: SsnDEPARTMENT(Dno‾, Dname, Manager)key: Dno\begin{aligned}&\textsf{EMPLOYEE}(\underline{\text{Ssn}},\ \text{Ename},\ \text{Dno}) &&\text{key: Ssn}\\ &\textsf{DEPARTMENT}(\underline{\text{Dno}},\ \text{Dname},\ \text{Manager}) &&\text{key: Dno}\end{aligned}​EMPLOYEE(Ssn​, Ename, Dno)DEPARTMENT(Dno​, Dname, Manager)​​key: Ssnkey: Dno​

    The department fact is stored once. Dno remains in EMPLOYEE so the employee’s department is still represented. Joining the tables on Dno reconstructs the original employee–department information.

    Normalisation is not “split every big table”

    Use the dependencies to identify the repeated fact, preserve the relationship to it, and verify that joining the results cannot invent extra facts.

    The other informal guidelines

    The textbook also warns about unclear attribute meanings (a relation should describe one entity or relationship type), excessive NULLs (attributes that are often NULL belong in a separate relation) and spurious tuples (joins that invent rows; see a lossy split). Good individual normal forms are useful, but the relationships among the resulting tables must be correct too.

    Textbook §14.1, pp. 461–470.

    Functional dependencies

    Definition

    X→YX\to YX→Y: in every legal instance, any two rows that agree on all attributes in XXX must agree on all attributes in YYY. XXX is the determinant.

    RequirementDependencyDo not assume
    Each student has one recorded name.Sid→Name\text{Sid}\to\text{Name}Sid→NameName→Sid\text{Name}\to\text{Sid}Name→Sid
    Each course has one title.Cid→Title\text{Cid}\to\text{Title}Cid→TitleTitle→Cid\text{Title}\to\text{Cid}Title→Cid
    One grade per student–course pair.Sid,Cid→Grade\text{Sid},\text{Cid}\to\text{Grade}Sid,Cid→GradeSid→Grade\text{Sid}\to\text{Grade}Sid→Grade
    Each department has one manager.Dno→Manager\text{Dno}\to\text{Manager}Dno→ManagerManager→Dno\text{Manager}\to\text{Dno}Manager→Dno unless stated

    Reading the arrow correctly

    Dno→Manager\text{Dno}\to\text{Manager}Dno→Manager allows many departments to have the same manager. It says that one department cannot have two different recorded managers at the same time. The reverse dependency needs a separate business rule.

    If the problem tracks history, the determinant may need a date or period. Do not silently carry a “current state” dependency into a historical table.

    Trivial and nontrivial dependencies

    AB→AAB\to AAB→A is trivial because its right-hand side is already on the left. A→BA\to BA→B is nontrivial if BBB is not in AAA. When testing 3NF and BCNF, trivial dependencies do not create violations.

    Can a small data table prove an FD?

    It can disprove one: two rows with the same XXX and different YYY violate X→YX\to YX→Y. It cannot establish a permanent business rule merely because no violation appears in today’s rows. Exercise 14.26 deliberately asks which dependencies may hold.

    R(A,B): (1,x), (1,y), (2,y)A→B fails: the first two rows agree on A, differ on B.B→A fails: the last two rows agree on B, differ on A.\begin{aligned}&R(A,B):\ (1,x),\ (1,y),\ (2,y)\\ &A\to B\text{ fails: the first two rows agree on }A\text{, differ on }B.\\ &B\to A\text{ fails: the last two rows agree on }B\text{, differ on }A.\end{aligned}​R(A,B): (1,x), (1,y), (2,y)A→B fails: the first two rows agree on A, differ on B.B→A fails: the last two rows agree on B, differ on A.​

    Textbook §14.2, pp. 471–474.

    Attribute closure: the main calculation

    X+X^+X+ is everything that XXX determines under the given dependency set FFF, including XXX itself. Compute it by repeatedly applying dependencies whose entire left-hand side is already known.

    R(A,B,C,D,E),F={A→B, B→C, AC→D, D→E}R(A,B,C,D,E),\qquad F=\{A\to B,\ B\to C,\ AC\to D,\ D\to E\}R(A,B,C,D,E),F={A→B, B→C, AC→D, D→E}
    StepKnown attributesReason
    StartAAAStart with the requested set.
    1A,BA,BA,BA→BA\to BA→B
    2A,B,CA,B,CA,B,CB→CB\to CB→C
    3A,B,C,DA,B,C,DA,B,C,DAC→DAC\to DAC→D; both AAA and CCC are now known.
    4A,B,C,D,EA,B,C,D,EA,B,C,D,ED→ED\to ED→E

    Thus A+=ABCDEA^+=ABCDEA+=ABCDE. AAA determines every attribute, so AAA is a superkey. It is also minimal because the empty set determines no attributes under this FFF. Hence AAA is a candidate key.

    The closure recipe
    1. Write X+:=XX^+ := XX+:=X.
    2. For each U→VU\to VU→V, if all of UUU is in X+X^+X+, add VVV.
    3. Repeat until an entire pass adds nothing.
    4. Compare the result with the whole schema, or with the dependency you are trying to prove.

    Two uses. XXX is a superkey exactly when X+X^+X+ contains every attribute of the relation. FFF implies X→YX\to YX→Y exactly when YYY is contained in X+X^+X+.

    Try it

    With the same FFF, calculate B+B^+B+ and (AC)+(AC)^+(AC)+ before reading on.

    Answers

    B+=BCB^+=BCB+=BC, so BBB is not a superkey. (AC)+=ABCDE(AC)^+=ABCDE(AC)+=ABCDE, but ACACAC is not a candidate key because AAA alone already determines everything. A superkey can be larger than necessary.

    Watch out: for AC→DAC\to DAC→D, knowing only AAA is not enough unless you can first derive CCC. Never apply a composite left-hand side one attribute at a time.

    Textbook §15.1.1, Algorithm 15.1. Read this before finding keys.

    Finding all candidate keys

    A reliable search strategy

    Start with attributes that never occur on any right-hand side of the given FDs. Every key must contain them, because no dependency can create them. Compute their closure. If it is incomplete, try adding attributes until you obtain a superkey; then check minimality.

    To find all keys, explore the other minimal combinations too. Once you find a key, do not explore its supersets. The textbook’s delete-from-the-whole-schema algorithm finds one key, not necessarily every key.

    Worked exercise 14.27

    R(A,B,C,D,E),F={AB→C, CD→E, DE→B}R(A,B,C,D,E),\qquad F=\{AB\to C,\ CD\to E,\ DE\to B\}R(A,B,C,D,E),F={AB→C, CD→E, DE→B}

    Pause. Is ABABAB a candidate key? Is ABDABDABD? Find the remaining candidate keys.

    SetClosure / argumentConclusion
    ABABABAB→CAB\to CAB→C gives ABCABCABC. No DDD or EEE can be added.Not a superkey.
    ABDABDABDAB→CAB\to CAB→C, then CD→ECD\to ECD→E gives ABCDEABCDEABCDE.Candidate key.
    ACDACDACDCD→ECD\to ECD→E, then DE→BDE\to BDE→B gives ABCDEABCDEABCDE.Candidate key.
    ADEADEADEDE→BDE\to BDE→B, then AB→CAB\to CAB→C gives ABCDEABCDEABCDE.Candidate key.

    AAA and DDD never occur on the right, so both are compulsory. (AD)+=AD(AD)^+=AD(AD)+=AD. Adding any one of BBB, CCC or EEE gives a key. Each is minimal: remove AAA or DDD and it can never be recovered; remove the third attribute and only ADADAD remains. Thus the complete set is ABD, ACD, ADEABD,\ ACD,\ ADEABD, ACD, ADE. The full exercise is Exercise 14.27.

    Prime is not the same as primary

    Here every attribute belongs to at least one candidate key, so all five attributes are prime. If ABDABDABD is chosen as primary key, EEE is still prime because it belongs to ADEADEADE.

    Textbook §15.1; scheduled exercise 14.27, p. 499.

    Full, partial and transitive dependence

    ENROL(Sid, Cid, Grade, Sname, Ctitle, DeptNo, DeptName)Sid,Cid→GradeSid→Sname, DeptNoCid→CtitleDeptNo→DeptName\begin{aligned}&\textsf{ENROL}(\text{Sid},\ \text{Cid},\ \text{Grade},\ \text{Sname},\ \text{Ctitle},\ \text{DeptNo},\ \text{DeptName})\\ &\text{Sid},\text{Cid}\to\text{Grade}\qquad \text{Sid}\to\text{Sname},\,\text{DeptNo}\qquad \text{Cid}\to\text{Ctitle}\qquad \text{DeptNo}\to\text{DeptName}\end{aligned}​ENROL(Sid, Cid, Grade, Sname, Ctitle, DeptNo, DeptName)Sid,Cid→GradeSid→Sname,DeptNoCid→CtitleDeptNo→DeptName​

    The only candidate key is {Sid, Cid}. Neither attribute appears on the right of these FDs, so both are required. Together they determine every column.

    Three kinds of dependence
    KindExampleWhy
    Full dependencySid,Cid→Grade\text{Sid},\text{Cid}\to\text{Grade}Sid,Cid→GradeNo proper subset of the pair determines Grade under these rules.
    Partial dependencySid,Cid→Sname\text{Sid},\text{Cid}\to\text{Sname}Sid,Cid→SnameSid alone determines Sname; Cid is unnecessary.
    Transitive pathSid→DeptNo→DeptName\text{Sid}\to\text{DeptNo}\to\text{DeptName}Sid→DeptNo→DeptNameThe department name is reached through DeptNo. In a student table, DeptNo is not a superkey and DeptName is nonprime.

    Dependency diagram

    (Sid, Cid) ───────────────→ Grade
Sid ─────────→ Sname
Sid ─────────→ DeptNo ─────────→ DeptName
Cid ────→ Ctitle

    The diagram shows why Grade belongs to the pair, Sname and DeptNo belong to a student, and DeptName belongs to a department. Normalisation makes those distinctions explicit in the tables.

    Do not classify only by the shape of an arrow chain

    A chain through a candidate key does not automatically violate 3NF. Use the formal 3NF test when there are multiple candidate keys or overlapping keys.

    A partial dependency is defined relative to a particular determinant. A 2NF violation specifically involves a nonprime attribute depending on a proper subset of a candidate key. Dependencies involving only prime attributes need more careful treatment.

    Textbook §§14.3–14.4. Assume the stated FDs are the relevant business rules.

    3  Normal forms · Ch. 14.3–14.5

    First and second normal forms

    1NF: one value in each attribute position

    A relation in 1NF has no repeating groups or set-valued/nested attributes. For the textbook exercises, treat values as atomic in their intended domains.

    Not 1NF: STUDENT(Sid, Name, {Phone})Use: STUDENT(Sid, Name) and STUDENT_PHONE(Sid, Phone)\begin{aligned}&\text{Not 1NF: }\textsf{STUDENT}(\text{Sid},\ \text{Name},\ \{\text{Phone}\})\\ &\text{Use: }\textsf{STUDENT}(\text{Sid},\ \text{Name})\text{ and }\textsf{STUDENT\_PHONE}(\text{Sid},\ \text{Phone})\end{aligned}​Not 1NF: STUDENT(Sid, Name, {Phone})Use: STUDENT(Sid, Name) and STUDENT_PHONE(Sid, Phone)​

    A long string is not automatically non-atomic. A phone list packed into one string is a poor way to represent multiple phone facts; the issue is the intended meaning and operations, not merely the storage type.

    2NF: no partial dependency of a nonprime attribute

    A 1NF relation is in 2NF if every nonprime attribute is fully dependent on every candidate key. No proper subset of any candidate key may determine a nonprime attribute.

    R(Sid, Cid, Grade, Sname, Ctitle)Key: Sid, Cid;Sid→Sname;Cid→Ctitle;Sid,Cid→Grade\begin{aligned}&R(\text{Sid},\ \text{Cid},\ \text{Grade},\ \text{Sname},\ \text{Ctitle})\\ &\text{Key: Sid, Cid;}\quad \text{Sid}\to\text{Sname};\quad \text{Cid}\to\text{Ctitle};\quad \text{Sid},\text{Cid}\to\text{Grade}\end{aligned}​R(Sid, Cid, Grade, Sname, Ctitle)Key: Sid, Cid;Sid→Sname;Cid→Ctitle;Sid,Cid→Grade​

    Sname depends on only Sid and Ctitle on only Cid. Both are nonprime, so RRR fails 2NF. Split it into:

    STUDENT(Sid‾, Sname)key: SidCOURSE(Cid‾, Ctitle)key: CidENROLMENT(Sid, Cid‾, Grade)key: Sid, Cid\begin{aligned}&\textsf{STUDENT}(\underline{\text{Sid}},\ \text{Sname}) &&\text{key: Sid}\\ &\textsf{COURSE}(\underline{\text{Cid}},\ \text{Ctitle}) &&\text{key: Cid}\\ &\textsf{ENROLMENT}(\underline{\text{Sid},\ \text{Cid}},\ \text{Grade}) &&\text{key: Sid, Cid}\end{aligned}​STUDENT(Sid​, Sname)COURSE(Cid​, Ctitle)ENROLMENT(Sid, Cid​, Grade)​​key: Sidkey: Cidkey: Sid, Cid​

    Keep ENROLMENT. Dropping the table containing the original pair would lose which student took which course and the grade attached to that pair.

    The single-column primary-key trap

    If all candidate keys are single attributes, 1NF implies 2NF under the ordinary nonconstant-dependency assumptions used here. A single-column primary key alone is not enough: another candidate key might be composite and have a partial dependency. LOTS demonstrates this.

    Textbook §§14.3–14.4. General definitions consider every candidate key.

    Third normal form, including the exception

    The intuitive case

    STUDENT(Sid, Sname, DeptNo, DeptName)Sid→Sname, DeptNo;DeptNo→DeptName\begin{aligned}&\textsf{STUDENT}(\text{Sid},\ \text{Sname},\ \text{DeptNo},\ \text{DeptName})\\ &\text{Sid}\to\text{Sname},\,\text{DeptNo};\qquad \text{DeptNo}\to\text{DeptName}\end{aligned}​STUDENT(Sid, Sname, DeptNo, DeptName)Sid→Sname,DeptNo;DeptNo→DeptName​

    Sid is the only candidate key. This relation is in 2NF, but DeptNo→DeptName\text{DeptNo}\to\text{DeptName}DeptNo→DeptName repeats a department fact. DeptNo is not a superkey and DeptName is nonprime, so this dependency violates 3NF.

    STUDENT(Sid‾, Sname, DeptNo)key: SidDEPARTMENT(DeptNo‾, DeptName)key: DeptNo\begin{aligned}&\textsf{STUDENT}(\underline{\text{Sid}},\ \text{Sname},\ \text{DeptNo}) &&\text{key: Sid}\\ &\textsf{DEPARTMENT}(\underline{\text{DeptNo}},\ \text{DeptName}) &&\text{key: DeptNo}\end{aligned}​STUDENT(Sid​, Sname, DeptNo)DEPARTMENT(DeptNo​, DeptName)​​key: Sidkey: DeptNo​
    The definition you should actually use

    For every nontrivial dependency X→AX\to AX→A that holds, a 1NF relation is in 3NF if at least one is true:

    1. XXX is a superkey.
    2. AAA is prime, meaning it occurs in some candidate key.

    Split a multi-attribute right-hand side into single attributes when applying the test. If the formal test passes, the relation already satisfies 2NF. You do not have to demonstrate each lower form separately unless the question asks for successive normalisation.

    Why the shortcut is not the full definition

    “No non-key →\to→ non-key” is useful intuition for simple examples with one key. It can mislead you when keys overlap. An FD whose determinant is not a superkey can still be allowed by 3NF when the attribute on the right is prime.

    A quick test

    R(A,B,C)R(A,B,C)R(A,B,C) has FDs AB→CAB\to CAB→C and C→BC\to BC→B. Its keys are ABABAB and ACACAC. Is C→BC\to BC→B a 3NF violation?

    Answer

    No. CCC is not a superkey, but BBB belongs to candidate key ABABAB and is therefore prime. This relation is in 3NF. It fails the stricter form on the next page.

    Textbook §14.4.2, p. 486.

    BCNF and the 3NF tradeoff

    Definition

    A 1NF relation is in BCNF if every nontrivial FD X→AX\to AX→A that holds has XXX as a superkey. There is no prime-attribute exception.

    TEACH: in 3NF but not BCNF
    TEACH(Student, Course, Instructor),Student,Course→Instructor,Instructor→Course\textsf{TEACH}(\text{Student},\ \text{Course},\ \text{Instructor}),\qquad \text{Student},\text{Course}\to\text{Instructor},\qquad \text{Instructor}\to\text{Course}TEACH(Student, Course, Instructor),Student,Course→Instructor,Instructor→Course

    Assumptions: each student has one instructor per course; each instructor teaches only one course. The candidate keys are {Student, Course} and {Student, Instructor}. All three attributes are prime.

    FD3NF testBCNF test
    Student,Course→Instructor\text{Student},\text{Course}\to\text{Instructor}Student,Course→InstructorPass: determinant is a key.Pass.
    Instructor→Course\text{Instructor}\to\text{Course}Instructor→CoursePass: Course is prime.Fail: Instructor does not determine Student.

    Decompose on the violating dependency

    IC(Instructor‾, Course)key: InstructorSI(Student, Instructor‾)key: Student, Instructor\begin{aligned}&\textsf{IC}(\underline{\text{Instructor}},\ \text{Course}) &&\text{key: Instructor}\\ &\textsf{SI}(\underline{\text{Student},\ \text{Instructor}}) &&\text{key: Student, Instructor}\end{aligned}​IC(Instructor​, Course)SI(Student, Instructor​)​​key: Instructorkey: Student, Instructor​

    Both results are in BCNF. The shared attribute Instructor determines all of IC, so the join is lossless. But Student,Course→Instructor\text{Student},\text{Course}\to\text{Instructor}Student,Course→Instructor is not preserved by the FDs inside these two tables.

    For example, SI could contain (S1, I1) and (S1, I2), while IC contains (I1, C1) and (I2, C1). Each table obeys its local dependencies. Their join assigns two instructors to student S1 in course C1, violating the original dependency.

    Tradeoff

    A standard 3NF synthesis can guarantee losslessness and dependency preservation. A BCNF decomposition guarantees losslessness, but cannot always preserve all FDs. BCNF does not automatically mean a better choice for every constraint-enforcement requirement.

    Textbook §14.5 and §15.3.2. TEACH example adapted from Figure 14.14.

    How to answer a normal-form question

    A repeatable answer structure
    1. Write the schema and the given FDs. State any needed business assumptions.
    2. Compute all candidate keys, with closure and minimality evidence.
    3. Mark prime and nonprime attributes.
    4. Identify the highest normal form and name an FD that violates the next one.
    5. Decompose using that FD. List each resulting schema and its keys.
    6. Re-test each result using the dependencies that hold on it.
    7. Justify losslessness and discuss dependency preservation if asked.
    What the grader checks
    ClaimEvidence you should write
    “ABABAB is a key.”(AB)+(AB)^+(AB)+ = all attributes; neither AAA nor BBB alone determines them all.
    “Fails 2NF.”A proper subset of a stated candidate key determines a specific nonprime attribute.
    “Fails 3NF.”For X→AX\to AX→A, XXX is not a superkey and AAA is nonprime.
    “3NF but not BCNF.”A violating determinant is not a superkey, but its RHS attribute is prime; all other relevant FDs pass 3NF.
    “Lossless.”Show the common attributes determine one component, or show an all-aaa tableau row.
    Mistakes that cost marks
    • Testing only the primary key and forgetting alternative candidate keys.
    • Calling a nonminimal superkey a candidate key.
    • Splitting a table without retaining the columns that link the facts back together.
    • Assuming all FDs disappear when their original table is split. Implied dependencies may still hold on a component.
    • Saying “all tables are in BCNF” as if that proves the decomposition is lossless.
    What holds on a component

    A component inherits the projection of F+F^+F+ onto its attributes. This includes dependencies implied through attributes outside that component. Recompute its keys rather than copying the original key mechanically.

    Use the formal tests; textbook §§14.3–14.5.

    4  Chapter 15 methods · Ch. 15.1–15.3

    Armstrong’s rules and equivalent FD sets

    Armstrong’s rules
    RuleStatementExample
    ReflexivityIf YYY is contained in XXX, then X→YX\to YX→Y.AB→AAB\to AAB→A
    AugmentationX→YX\to YX→Y implies XZ→YZXZ\to YZXZ→YZ.A→BA\to BA→B implies AC→BCAC\to BCAC→BC.
    TransitivityX→YX\to YX→Y and Y→ZY\to ZY→Z imply X→ZX\to ZX→Z.A→B, B→CA\to B,\ B\to CA→B, B→C imply A→CA\to CA→C.

    These rules are sound: they derive only dependencies implied by the starting rules. They are complete: every implied FD can be derived using them.

    Useful derived rules

    RuleStatement
    UnionX→YX\to YX→Y and X→ZX\to ZX→Z imply X→YZX\to YZX→YZ.
    DecompositionX→YZX\to YZX→YZ implies X→YX\to YX→Y and X→ZX\to ZX→Z.
    PseudotransitivityX→YX\to YX→Y and WY→ZWY\to ZWY→Z imply WX→ZWX\to ZWX→Z.

    F+F^+F+ is different from X+X^+X+

    F+F^+F+ contains dependencies, including all implied ones. X+X^+X+ contains attributes determined by one starting attribute set. You usually compute attribute closures rather than explicitly listing the enormous set F+F^+F+.

    Equivalent sets express the same constraints
    F={A→B, B→C}G={A→B, B→C, A→C}F=\{A\to B,\ B\to C\}\qquad G=\{A\to B,\ B\to C,\ A\to C\}F={A→B, B→C}G={A→B, B→C, A→C}

    GGG contains an extra written rule, but A→CA\to CA→C already follows from FFF. Thus F+=G+F^+=G^+F+=G+. To test equivalence generally, check every FD in FFF using closures under GGG, then every FD in GGG using closures under FFF.

    Do both directions

    Showing FFF implies GGG alone does not prove equivalence. GGG could be weaker and fail to imply some rule in FFF.

    Textbook §15.1, pp. 505–510.

    Minimal covers, one reduction at a time

    A minimal cover is an equivalent FD set with singleton right-hand sides, no extraneous left-hand attributes and no redundant dependencies. It need not be unique.

    The algorithm
    1. Split every right-hand side: A→BCA\to BCA→BC becomes A→BA\to BA→B and A→CA\to CA→C.
    2. For X→AX\to AX→A, test each BBB in XXX. If AAA is in (X−{B})+(X-\{B\})^+(X−{B})+ under the current FFF, BBB is extraneous; shorten the left side.
    3. For each remaining X→AX\to AX→A, temporarily remove that FD. If AAA is still in X+X^+X+ under the remaining set, delete the FD.
    4. Make one change at a time and recheck the current set. Group equal left sides for presentation if useful.

    Worked reduction

    E={B→A, D→A, AB→D}E=\{B\to A,\ D\to A,\ AB\to D\}E={B→A, D→A, AB→D}

    Step 1. Right-hand sides are already single attributes.

    Step 2. Test whether AAA is extraneous in AB→DAB\to DAB→D. Starting with BBB, B→AB\to AB→A gives ABABAB; then AB→DAB\to DAB→D gives DDD. Thus B→DB\to DB→D already follows. Replace AB→DAB\to DAB→D with B→DB\to DB→D.

    Current set={B→A, D→A, B→D}\text{Current set}=\{B\to A,\ D\to A,\ B\to D\}Current set={B→A, D→A, B→D}

    Step 3. Temporarily remove B→AB\to AB→A. B→DB\to DB→D and D→AD\to AD→A still derive it. Delete B→AB\to AB→A.

    Answer

    Minimal cover G={B→D, D→A}G=\{B\to D,\ D\to A\}G={B→D, D→A}.

    Equivalence check. EEE implies B→DB\to DB→D by the closure above, and contains D→AD\to AD→A. GGG implies B→AB\to AB→A transitively and AB→DAB\to DAB→D by augmentation/decomposition. Neither FD in GGG is removable.

    The two closure tests use different sets

    For an extraneous LHS attribute, use the current FFF. For a redundant FD, remove that FD before testing. Leaving it in would make every FD appear redundant. Because each change alters the current set, the order of reductions can lead to a different (equally valid) minimal cover.

    Textbook §15.1.3, Algorithm 15.2; example based on pp. 511–512.

    Lossless joins: do we get the same facts back?

    A projection keeps selected columns and removes duplicate rows. A natural join combines rows that agree on every common column. Normalisation must allow the original relation to be reconstructed exactly by joining its projections.

    Lossless

    Lossless means no information is lost. A lossy decomposition typically produces extra, spurious rows when joined. It is not simply about losing row counts.

    Binary test: one split into two tables

    Let I=R1∩R2I=R_1\cap R_2I=R1​∩R2​, the shared attributes. The decomposition is lossless under FFF if and only if I→R1I\to R_1I→R1​ or I→R2I\to R_2I→R2​ follows from FFF. Compute I+I^+I+ to test this. Assume R1∪R2R_1\cup R_2R1​∪R2​ contains all original attributes.

    R(A,B,C), F={A→B}Split: R1(A,B), R2(A,C)Intersection=A; A+=AB; contains R1⇒lossless.\begin{aligned}&R(A,B,C),\ F=\{A\to B\}\\ &\text{Split: }R_1(A,B),\ R_2(A,C)\\ &\text{Intersection}=A;\ A^+=AB\text{; contains }R_1\Rightarrow\text{lossless.}\end{aligned}​R(A,B,C), F={A→B}Split: R1​(A,B), R2​(A,C)Intersection=A; A+=AB; contains R1​⇒lossless.​
    A lossy split you can see
    Original R: (a1,b,c1), (a2,b,c2)R1(A,B): (a1,b), (a2,b)R2(B,C): (b,c1), (b,c2)\begin{aligned}&\text{Original }R:\ (a_1,b,c_1),\ (a_2,b,c_2)\\ &R_1(A,B):\ (a_1,b),\ (a_2,b)\\ &R_2(B,C):\ (b,c_1),\ (b,c_2)\end{aligned}​Original R: (a1​,b,c1​), (a2​,b,c2​)R1​(A,B): (a1​,b), (a2​,b)R2​(B,C): (b,c1​), (b,c2​)​

    The join also creates (a1,b,c2)(a_1,b,c_2)(a1​,b,c2​) and (a2,b,c1)(a_2,b,c_1)(a2​,b,c1​). The common BBB does not tell us which AAA belongs with which CCC. With no FDs, BBB determines neither ABABAB nor BCBCBC, so the split fails the test.

    More than two components

    If each successive binary split is lossless, the whole decomposition is lossless. For an arbitrary multi-table decomposition, use the tableau/chase test. Checking intersections between a few arbitrary pairs is not a general proof.

    Losslessness is a statement about every legal instance satisfying FFF. One successful join on a tiny sample does not prove the property.

    Textbook §§14.5.1 and 15.2, especially the binary NJB test.

    Dependency preservation is a separate test

    A decomposition is dependency-preserving when the dependencies enforceable inside the component tables, taken together, imply all the original FDs. You should not need to join tables just to verify a dependency.

    An easy preserved case

    R(A,B,C);F={A→B, B→C};decompose into AB and BC.R(A,B,C);\quad F=\{A\to B,\ B\to C\};\quad\text{decompose into }AB\text{ and }BC.R(A,B,C);F={A→B, B→C};decompose into AB and BC.

    A→BA\to BA→B can be enforced in ABABAB, and B→CB\to CB→C in BCBCBC. Their union is already FFF, so the decomposition preserves dependencies. The intersection BBB determines BCBCBC, so it is also lossless. These are separate arguments.

    A lossless case that loses a constraint

    TEACH(S,C,I);F={SC→I, I→C};decompose into IC and SI.\textsf{TEACH}(S,C,I);\quad F=\{SC\to I,\ I\to C\};\quad\text{decompose into }IC\text{ and }SI.TEACH(S,C,I);F={SC→I, I→C};decompose into IC and SI.

    I→CI\to CI→C remains enforceable in ICICIC. SISISI has no nontrivial projected FDs. Starting from SCSCSC under the component dependencies cannot produce III, so SC→ISC\to ISC→I is not preserved. The split is nevertheless lossless because the shared III determines ICICIC.

    The general test

    Project F+F^+F+ onto each component: retain all implied FDs whose attributes fit inside that component. Let GGG be the union of those projected dependencies. For every original X→AX\to AX→A, check whether AAA belongs to X+X^+X+ under GGG. If any fails, the decomposition is not dependency-preserving.

    An FD need not appear verbatim in one table

    It can be preserved through a chain of local dependencies. For example, A→CA\to CA→C can be enforced indirectly when ABABAB enforces A→BA\to BA→B and BCBCBC enforces B→CB\to CB→C.

    Do not merely delete written FDs that cross component boundaries and assume the rest is the complete projection. Hidden implied FDs may matter. For small exercises, use closure calculations to identify them.

    Textbook §15.2.2. Compare the TEACH example.

    Constructing 3NF and BCNF designs

    3NF synthesis: preserve dependencies and losslessness
    1. Compute a minimal cover GGG.
    2. For each determinant XXX in GGG, create a table containing XXX and all attributes it determines in GGG.
    3. If no table contains a candidate key of the original relation, add a table containing one.
    4. Remove a table contained entirely inside another table.
    R(A,B,C,D); F={A→B, B→C}Minimal cover is already F. Candidate key: AD.Create AB and BC. Neither contains AD. Add AD.Result: AB, BC, AD.\begin{aligned}&R(A,B,C,D);\ F=\{A\to B,\ B\to C\}\\ &\text{Minimal cover is already }F.\ \text{Candidate key: }AD.\\ &\text{Create }AB\text{ and }BC.\ \text{Neither contains }AD.\ \text{Add }AD.\\ &\text{Result: }AB,\ BC,\ AD.\end{aligned}​R(A,B,C,D); F={A→B, B→C}Minimal cover is already F. Candidate key: AD.Create AB and BC. Neither contains AD. Add AD.Result: AB, BC, AD.​

    Each result is BCNF here: ABABAB has key AAA, BCBCBC has key BBB, and ADADAD has no nontrivial FDs. Every original FD is local. Losslessness also follows successively: split RRR into BCBCBC and ABDABDABD using B→CB\to CB→C, then ABDABDABD into ABABAB and ADADAD using A→BA\to BA→B.

    BCNF decomposition: split on a violating FD

    For a component QQQ with a nontrivial FD X→YX\to YX→Y where XXX is not a superkey, first remove attributes of XXX from YYY. Replace QQQ with X∪YX\cup YX∪Y and Q−YQ-YQ−Y. Repeat until every component is in BCNF.

    Always use the dependencies that hold on the current component, including implied ones. Each split is lossless because the intersection XXX determines X∪YX\cup YX∪Y. Dependency preservation requires a separate check.

    R(A,B,C); F={AB→C, C→B}C→B violates BCNF. Split into CB and AC.CB key: C; AC key: AC. Both BCNF.Lossless, but AB→C is not preserved.\begin{aligned}&R(A,B,C);\ F=\{AB\to C,\ C\to B\}\\ &C\to B\text{ violates BCNF. Split into }CB\text{ and }AC.\\ &CB\text{ key: }C;\ AC\text{ key: }AC.\ \text{Both BCNF.}\\ &\text{Lossless, but }AB\to C\text{ is not preserved.}\end{aligned}​R(A,B,C); F={AB→C, C→B}C→B violates BCNF. Split into CB and AC.CB key: C; AC key: AC. Both BCNF.Lossless, but AB→C is not preserved.​
    When the question says “successively into 2NF, then 3NF”

    Show those intermediate stages. Synthesis is a direct construction method and does not replace explicitly requested intermediate answers.

    Textbook §15.3, Algorithms 15.4–15.5. Optional 10-minute block.

    5  Worked scheduled problems

    Worked 14.24: from keys to 3NF

    R(A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H,I,J);AB→C;  A→DE;  B→F;  F→GH;  D→IJR(A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H,I,J);\qquad AB\to C;\ \ A\to DE;\ \ B\to F;\ \ F\to GH;\ \ D\to IJR(A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H,I,J);AB→C;  A→DE;  B→F;  F→GH;  D→IJ

    Try first. Find the key. Then separate partial dependencies before removing the remaining transitive dependencies. The full exercise is Exercise 14.24.

    1. Candidate key

    AAA and BBB never occur on a right-hand side, so every key contains both. (AB)+(AB)^+(AB)+ adds CCC from ABABAB, DEDEDE from AAA, FFF from BBB, GHGHGH from FFF and IJIJIJ from DDD. Thus (AB)+(AB)^+(AB)+ is all attributes. Removing AAA or BBB cannot work. The only candidate key is ABABAB; only AAA and BBB are prime.

    2. Into 2NF

    AAA alone determines DEIJDEIJDEIJ and BBB alone determines FGHFGHFGH. These are partial dependencies on key ABABAB. CCC needs the full pair.

    R1(A,B‾,C)R2(A‾,D,E,I,J)R3(B‾,F,G,H)R_1(\underline{A,B},C)\quad R_2(\underline{A},D,E,I,J)\quad R_3(\underline{B},F,G,H)R1​(A,B​,C)R2​(A​,D,E,I,J)R3​(B​,F,G,H)

    R1R_1R1​ is BCNF. R2R_2R2​ and R3R_3R3​ are 2NF because their only candidate keys are single attributes, but D→IJD\to IJD→IJ and F→GHF\to GHF→GH still violate 3NF.

    3. Into 3NF

    Answer
    AB‾CA‾DEB‾FF‾GHD‾IJ\underline{AB}C\quad \underline{A}DE\quad \underline{B}F\quad \underline{F}GH\quad \underline{D}IJAB​CA​DEB​FF​GHD​IJ

    Every component is actually BCNF under the projected dependencies. All original FDs are local, so the result preserves dependencies.

    Losslessness. First split off ADEIJADEIJADEIJ using A→DEIJA\to DEIJA→DEIJ, leaving ABCFGHABCFGHABCFGH. Split off BFGHBFGHBFGH using B→FGHB\to FGHB→FGH, leaving ABCABCABC. Then split ADEIJADEIJADEIJ on D→IJD\to IJD→IJ and BFGHBFGHBFGH on F→GHF\to GHF→GH. Every shared determinant determines one side of its split, so the full decomposition is lossless.

    Worked 14.30: partial, then transitive

    CAR_SALE(Car, Date, Salesperson, Commission, Discount),key given: Car, SalespersonCar,Salesperson→DateSalesperson→CommissionDate→Discount\begin{aligned}&\textsf{CAR\_SALE}(\text{Car},\ \text{Date},\ \text{Salesperson},\ \text{Commission},\ \text{Discount}),\quad\text{key given: Car, Salesperson}\\ &\text{Car},\text{Salesperson}\to\text{Date}\qquad \text{Salesperson}\to\text{Commission}\qquad \text{Date}\to\text{Discount}\end{aligned}​CAR_SALE(Car, Date, Salesperson, Commission, Discount),key given: Car, SalespersonCar,Salesperson→DateSalesperson→CommissionDate→Discount​

    Use only the stated dependencies and the given key. Do not assume Car→Date\text{Car}\to\text{Date}Car→Date just because it seems plausible. The exercise allows multiple salespeople per car. The full exercise is Exercise 14.30.

    What is its highest normal form?

    Assume atomic values, so it is in 1NF. Car and Salesperson are required in every key because neither appears on an FD right-hand side. Their pair determines everything, so it is the only candidate key.

    Salesperson→Commission\text{Salesperson}\to\text{Commission}Salesperson→Commission is a dependency of a nonprime attribute on a proper subset of the key. Therefore the original relation fails 2NF and its highest normal form is 1NF.

    First make it 2NF

    SP(Salesperson‾, Commission)SALE(Car, Salesperson‾, Date, Discount)\textsf{SP}(\underline{\text{Salesperson}},\ \text{Commission})\qquad \textsf{SALE}(\underline{\text{Car},\ \text{Salesperson}},\ \text{Date},\ \text{Discount})SP(Salesperson​, Commission)SALE(Car, Salesperson​, Date, Discount)

    SP is BCNF. SALE is 2NF, but Date→Discount\text{Date}\to\text{Discount}Date→Discount violates 3NF: Date is not a superkey, and Discount is nonprime.

    Then make it 3NF

    Answer
    SP(Salesperson‾, Commission)SALE(Car, Salesperson‾, Date)DD(Date‾, Discount)\textsf{SP}(\underline{\text{Salesperson}},\ \text{Commission})\quad \textsf{SALE}(\underline{\text{Car},\ \text{Salesperson}},\ \text{Date})\quad \textsf{DD}(\underline{\text{Date}},\ \text{Discount})SP(Salesperson​, Commission)SALE(Car, Salesperson​, Date)DD(Date​, Discount)

    All three components are BCNF with the stated assumptions. Every original FD is represented locally.

    Lossless in two steps

    In the first split, shared Salesperson determines SP. In the second, shared Date determines DD. The original car–salesperson pair remains together in SALE, preserving who participated in the sale.

    The full exercise is Exercise 15.21.

    (a) Which proposed sets are candidate keys?

    SetClosureAnswer
    MMMM, MP, CM,\ MP,\ CM, MP, CNo YYY or PPP: not a superkey.
    MYMYMYM, Y, MP, C, PM,\ Y,\ MP,\ C,\ PM, Y, MP, C, PA candidate key.
    MCMCMCM, C, MPM,\ C,\ MPM, C, MPNo YYY or PPP: not a superkey.

    MMM and YYY do not occur on the right-hand sides, so every key must contain them. MYMYMY determines everything and neither attribute can be dropped. Hence MYMYMY is the only candidate key; MMM and YYY are prime.

    (b) Is REFRIG in 3NF or BCNF?

    No. M→MPM\to MPM→MP violates 2NF because MPMPMP is nonprime and MMM is a proper subset of key MYMYMY. It also fails the formal 3NF test: MMM is not a superkey and MPMPMP is nonprime. MP→CMP\to CMP→C is another 3NF/BCNF violation. Assuming atomic values, the highest form is 1NF.

    (c) Is the proposed split lossless?

    Exercise 15.24: binary losslessness proof

    Split LOTS into CTCTCT and PCLAVPCLAVPCLAV, with intersection CCC and C→TC\to TC→T. Split the latter into AVAVAV and PCLAPCLAPCLA, with intersection AAA and A→VA\to VA→V. Finally split PCLAPCLAPCLA into ACACAC and PALPALPAL, with intersection AAA and A→CA\to CA→C. Each binary split is lossless; therefore the final four-table design is lossless. The full exercise is Exercise 15.24.

    Dependency warning

    All four results are BCNF, but CL→PCL\to PCL→P is not preserved. Under their local dependencies, CLCLCL yields TTT but cannot yield AAA or PPP. The next page proves losslessness independently using the requested tableau.

    Worked tableau for exercise 15.24

    The tableau test

    Make one row per component, one column per original attribute. If a component contains a column, enter that column’s distinguished symbol, such as aPa_PaP​. Otherwise enter a fresh bbb symbol unique to that cell. Then chase: rows that agree on an FD’s whole LHS must agree on its RHS. Prefer the column’s aaa symbol when one is present; otherwise unify the bbb symbols consistently everywhere they occur. An all-aaa row proves losslessness; if the process stabilises with no all-aaa row, the FD-based test fails.

    1. Apply A→CA\to CA→C. Rows PAL, AC and AV agree on A=aAA=a_AA=aA​. Make their CCC symbols equal. AC has aCa_CaC​, so use aCa_CaC​. In particular, PAL’s b1Cb_{1C}b1C​ becomes aCa_CaC​.
    2. Apply A→VA\to VA→V. Those same three rows agree on AAA. AV has aVa_VaV​, so make their VVV entries aVa_VaV​. PAL’s b1Vb_{1V}b1V​ becomes aVa_VaV​.
    3. Apply C→TC\to TC→T. All four rows now agree on C=aCC=a_CC=aC​. CT has aTa_TaT​, so their TTT entries become aTa_TaT​. PAL’s b1Tb_{1T}b1T​ becomes aTa_TaT​.
    ComponentPCLAVT
    PALaPa_PaP​aCa_CaC​aLa_LaL​aAa_AaA​aVa_VaV​aTa_TaT​
    ACb2Pb_{2P}b2P​aCa_CaC​b2Lb_{2L}b2L​aAa_AaA​aVa_VaV​aTa_TaT​
    AVb3Pb_{3P}b3P​aCa_CaC​b3Lb_{3L}b3L​aAa_AaA​aVa_VaV​aTa_TaT​
    CTb4Pb_{4P}b4P​aCa_CaC​b4Lb_{4L}b4L​b4Ab_{4A}b4A​b4Vb_{4V}b4V​aTa_TaT​
    Answer

    The PAL row is entirely distinguished aaa symbols. Therefore the decomposition is lossless. You may stop as soon as a complete all-aaa row appears; there is no need to chase every FD afterwards.

    Textbook Algorithm 15.3. Same LOTS assumptions and symbols as the previous page.

    6  Extension: MVDs, 4NF and 5NF · Ch. 14.6–14.7, 15.5

    BCNF does not catch every kind of redundancy

    Suppose a student has a set of hobbies and a set of languages, and the two sets are independent. Putting both sets in one atomic-valued table repeats their combinations.

    StudentHobbyLanguage
    S1ChessEnglish
    S1ChessHindi
    S1MusicEnglish
    S1MusicHindi

    Student does not functionally determine a single Hobby or Language. Instead, for each student, their hobbies vary independently of their languages. This is a multivalued dependency, Student↠Hobby\text{Student}\twoheadrightarrow\text{Hobby}Student↠Hobby, and symmetrically Student↠Language\text{Student}\twoheadrightarrow\text{Language}Student↠Language.

    4NF

    For every nontrivial MVD X↠YX\twoheadrightarrow YX↠Y, XXX must be a superkey. An MVD is trivial if YYY is contained in XXX or X∪YX\cup YX∪Y is the whole relation.

    With only the independence rules above, the three-column table has no nontrivial FDs and is BCNF. It fails 4NF because Student is not a superkey. Decompose it losslessly into STUDENT_HOBBY(Student, Hobby) and STUDENT_LANGUAGE(Student, Language).

    Independence is the assumption that matters

    If a hobby is specifically practised in a particular language, those pairings are meaningful. Splitting them into two independent lists would lose that meaning. Do not infer an MVD merely because one person has several values in two columns.

    5NF: join dependencies

    A join dependency says that a relation always equals the join of certain projections. A relation is in 5NF when every nontrivial join dependency is implied by its candidate keys. Some valid decompositions require three or more projections and cannot be justified just by an FD or an MVD.

    Know the meaning and purpose for recognition. Unless your lecturer emphasised it, spend your limited practice time on candidate keys, 3NF/BCNF and lossless decomposition first.

    Textbook §§14.6–14.7 and §15.5. Lower priority for the 150-minute route.

    7  Chapter 14 review questions

    Textbook exercises

    14.2Update anomaliesE&N Ex. 14.2 · p. 496★ Must-do

    Discuss insertion, deletion, and modification anomalies. Why are they considered bad? Illustrate with examples.

    Solution · written for this guide

    Update anomalies arise when a base relation stores facts about several things together (typically a stored join), so the same fact is repeated in many tuples. Example: EMP_DEPT(Ename, Ssn, Bdate, Address, Dnumber, Dname, Dmgr_ssn), where (Dnumber, Dname, Dmgr_ssn) is repeated for every employee of the department.

    SsnDnumberDnameDmgr_ssn
    1234567895Research333445555
    3334455555Research333445555
    6668844445Research333445555
    8886655551Headquarters888665555
    AnomalyDefinitionEMP_DEPT example
    InsertionCannot insert a fact without also inserting (or NULL-padding) an unrelated fact, or must re-enter repeated data consistently.(a) A new employee of dept. 5 must carry Research/333445555 exactly as in the other dept. 5 tuples. (b) A new department with no employees can only be inserted with Ssn NULL, which entity integrity forbids.
    DeletionDeleting one fact unintentionally deletes another.Deleting Borg (the only employee of dept. 1) loses the fact that department 1 is Headquarters managed by 888665555.
    ModificationChanging one fact requires updating many tuples; missing one leaves inconsistent data.A new manager for dept. 5 must be written into every dept. 5 employee tuple; if one is missed, dept. 5 has two managers.

    Similarly in EMP_PROJ(Ssn, Pnumber, Hours, Ename, Pname, Plocation): a project with no workers cannot be inserted (Ssn is part of the key), deleting the last worker of a project loses the project, and renaming a project means updating every WORKS_ON row for it.

    Why bad: they waste storage (redundancy), make updates expensive and error-prone, risk inconsistency (the database contradicts itself), and cause accidental loss of information. In the normalized design EMPLOYEE(Ssn, …, Dnumber), DEPARTMENT(Dnumber, Dname, Dmgr_ssn) each department fact is stored once, so none of the three anomalies occurs. (Guideline 2: design base relations without anomalies; if some are kept for performance, document them and handle them in the update programs.)

    Answer

    Insertion, deletion and modification anomalies are side effects of redundancy: you cannot insert, delete or change one fact independently of others. They waste space, invite inconsistency and lose information, so base relations should be decomposed (normalized) to remove them.

    14.3NULLs and spurious tuplesE&N Ex. 14.3 · p. 496

    Why should NULLs in a relation be avoided as much as possible? Discuss the problem of spurious tuples and how we may prevent it.

    Solution · written for this guide

    NULLs

    • Storage: a “fat” relation with attributes that apply to few tuples wastes space.
    • Meaning is ambiguous: NULL may mean not applicable (Visa_status of a citizen), unknown (a missing birth date) or exists but not recorded (a home phone not on file); one NULL cannot say which.
    • Joins: tuples with NULL join attributes vanish from inner joins; inner and outer joins then give different answers.
    • Aggregates and conditions: COUNT, SUM, AVG ignore NULLs; comparisons with NULL are unknown (three-valued logic), so results can surprise.

    Remedy (Guideline 3): move rarely-applicable attributes to a separate relation, e.g. EMP_OFFICES(Essn, Office_number) holding only employees who have an office.

    Spurious tuples

    Spurious tuples are tuples that appear in the natural join of decomposed relations but were not in the original relation; they represent false information. Example: splitting EMP_PROJ into EMP_LOCS(Ename, Plocation) and EMP_PROJ1(Ssn, Pnumber, Hours, Pname, Plocation) and joining on Plocation pairs every project at Bellaire with every employee who works at Bellaire, e.g. (123456789, 1, 32.5, ProductX, Bellaire, English). The cause: the join attribute Plocation is neither a primary key nor a foreign key, so it does not identify a unique partner tuple.

    Prevention (Guideline 4): design relations that are joined on (primary key, foreign key) pairs; formally, require the lossless (nonadditive) join property: for a binary split, R1∩R2R_1\cap R_2R1​∩R2​ must functionally determine R1−R2R_1-R_2R1​−R2​ or R2−R1R_2-R_1R2​−R1​ (the common attributes are a key of one side), checked with NJB or the chase (Algorithm 15.3). Here {Plocation}+={Plocation}\{\textsf{Plocation}\}^+=\{\textsf{Plocation}\}{Plocation}+={Plocation}, so the split fails the test.

    Answer

    Avoid NULLs because they waste space, have unclear meaning, and break joins and aggregates. Spurious tuples are wrong tuples created by joining on attributes that are not PK–FK pairs; prevent them by decomposing only losslessly (common attributes are a key of one of the relations).

    14.4Informal design guidelinesE&N Ex. 14.4 · p. 496

    State the informal guidelines for relation schema design that we discussed. Illustrate how violation of these guidelines may be harmful.

    Solution · written for this guide
    GuidelineStatementHarm when violated (example)
    1. Clear semanticsEach relation should be easy to explain; do not mix attributes of several entity/relationship types.EMP_DEPT mixes employees and departments: its meaning is muddled and it leads directly to the anomalies of guideline 2.
    2. No redundancy (no anomalies)Design base relations with no insertion, deletion or modification anomalies; if any remain, document them and make programs handle them.EMP_DEPT: cannot add an empty department; deleting the last employee loses the department; changing a manager needs many updates.
    3. Few NULLsAvoid attributes that are frequently NULL; NULLs should be exceptional.Office_number in EMPLOYEE (15% have offices): wasted space, ambiguous NULL meaning, wrong counts and lost tuples in joins.
    4. No spurious tuplesRelations should be joinable on (PK, FK) pairs so that joins generate no spurious tuples.EMP_LOCS ∗*∗ EMP_PROJ1 on Plocation produces employee–project pairs that never existed: queries return false information.

    The guidelines are informal; normalization (FDs, normal forms, lossless and dependency-preserving decomposition) makes 2 and 4 precise.

    Answer

    Clear semantics; no update anomalies (no redundancy); avoid frequent NULLs; no spurious tuples (join on PK–FK, lossless decompositions). Violations cause confusion, inconsistent updates, wasted space and wrong query results.

    14.5Functional dependency and its sourcesE&N Ex. 14.5 · p. 496

    What is a functional dependency? What are the possible sources of the information that defines the functional dependencies that hold among the attributes of a relation schema?

    Solution · written for this guide

    Definition

    For X,Y⊆RX,Y\subseteq RX,Y⊆R, the FD X→YX \rightarrow YX→Y is a constraint on all legal states rrr of RRR: for any tuples t1,t2∈rt_1,t_2\in rt1​,t2​∈r, t1[X]=t2[X]⇒t1[Y]=t2[Y]t_1[X]=t_2[X]\Rightarrow t_1[Y]=t_2[Y]t1​[X]=t2​[X]⇒t1​[Y]=t2​[Y]. The XXX-value uniquely determines the YYY-value. Example in EMP_PROJ: Ssn→Ename\textsf{Ssn} \rightarrow \textsf{Ename}Ssn→Ename, Pnumber→{Pname,Plocation}\textsf{Pnumber} \rightarrow \{\textsf{Pname},\textsf{Plocation}\}Pnumber→{Pname,Plocation}, {Ssn,Pnumber}→Hours\{\textsf{Ssn},\textsf{Pnumber}\} \rightarrow \textsf{Hours}{Ssn,Pnumber}→Hours.

    Sources

    • The semantics (meaning) of the attributes, as understood by the designer from the application: requirements documents, business rules and policies (“each instructor teaches one course”), regulations and laws (“{State, Driver_license_number} →\to→ Ssn”), and domain experts / users.
    • Keys declared for the conceptual design (a key determines every attribute) and the structure of the ER model (an entity’s key determines its attributes; a 1:N relationship gives N-side key→1-side key\text{N-side key}\to\text{1-side key}N-side key→1-side key).
    • Inference: further FDs follow from the stated ones by Armstrong’s rules (they form F+F^+F+).

    Not a source: the data currently stored (see 14.6). FDs are properties of the schema and can change if the real world changes (Zip_code →\to→ Area_code once held in the U.S. but no longer does).

    Answer

    An FD X→YX \rightarrow YX→Y says equal XXX-values force equal YYY-values in every legal state. FDs come from the meaning of the data: requirements, business rules, laws and domain experts (plus key constraints and those inferred by Armstrong’s rules), never from a sample state.

    14.6FDs from a relation stateE&N Ex. 14.6 · p. 496

    Why can we not infer a functional dependency automatically from a particular relation state?

    Solution · written for this guide

    An FD must hold in every legal state of RRR, now and in the future, but a given state is one snapshot. If no two tuples violate X→YX \rightarrow YX→Y today, that may be a coincidence of the current data; a later legal insertion could violate it. So:

    • a state can only show that an FD may hold (no violating pair);
    • a state can show for certain that an FD does not hold (one violating pair is a counterexample).

    Example (TEACH state of Figure 14.7):

    TeacherCourseText
    SmithData StructuresBartram
    SmithData ManagementMartin
    HallCompilersHoffman
    BrownData StructuresHorowitz

    Text→Course\textsf{Text} \rightarrow \textsf{Course}Text→Course is not violated here, but we cannot conclude it holds (another course could use Bartram). Teacher→Course\textsf{Teacher} \rightarrow \textsf{Course}Teacher→Course certainly does not hold (Smith teaches two courses), nor does Course→Text\textsf{Course} \rightarrow \textsf{Text}Course→Text (Data Structures has two texts). Deciding which FDs hold requires knowing what the attributes mean.

    Answer

    Because an FD is a constraint on all possible legal states (a property of the schema’s semantics), while a state is one instance: data can refute an FD but never establish it.

    14.7Unnormalized relations; history of normal formsE&N Ex. 14.7 · p. 497

    What does the term unnormalized relation refer to? How did the normal forms develop historically from first normal form up to Boyce-Codd normal form?

    Solution · written for this guide

    Unnormalized relation

    A relation that is not in 1NF: some attribute holds non-atomic values (a set of values, a composite value, or a whole nested relation), e.g. DEPARTMENT(Dname, Dnumber, Dmgr_ssn, Dlocations) with Dlocations ={=\{={Bellaire, Sugarland, Houston}\}}, or EMP_PROJ(Ssn, Ename, {PROJS(Pnumber, Hours)}). (In a looser sense the term is also used for any relation not yet normalized to the desired form.)

    Historical development

    1. 1NF (Codd, 1970/72): attributes must be atomic and single-valued; now part of the definition of a flat relation.
    2. 2NF (Codd, 1972): based on full functional dependency; no non-prime attribute depends on part of the primary key.
    3. 3NF (Codd, 1972): 2NF plus no transitive dependency of a non-prime attribute on the primary key. 1NF and 2NF were proposed as stepping stones to 3NF. All three were first defined on the primary key, later generalized to all candidate keys.
    4. BCNF (Boyce and Codd, 1974): proposed as a simpler restatement of 3NF (every non-trivial FD has a superkey LHS) but turned out strictly stronger: it also forbids X→AX \rightarrow AX→A with XXX not a superkey and AAA prime.

    Later came 4NF (multivalued dependencies) and 5NF (join dependencies).

    Answer

    An unnormalized relation has non-atomic (multivalued, composite or nested) attribute values, i.e. is not in 1NF. Codd defined 1NF, 2NF (no partial dependencies) and 3NF (no transitive dependencies) in 1972 as successive steps; Boyce and Codd then defined the stricter BCNF (every determinant is a superkey).

    14.81NF, 2NF, 3NF on primary keys vs. generalE&N Ex. 14.8 · p. 497

    Define first, second, and third normal forms when only primary keys are considered. How do the general definitions of 2NF and 3NF, which consider all keys of a relation, differ from those that consider only primary keys?

    Solution · written for this guide

    Primary-key definitions

    • 1NF: every attribute value is atomic and single-valued (no multivalued/composite attributes, no nested relations).
    • 2NF: 1NF, and every non-prime attribute is fully functionally dependent on the primary key (no non-prime attribute depends on a proper part of the PK). Example: EMP_PROJ is not 2NF since Ssn→Ename\textsf{Ssn} \rightarrow \textsf{Ename}Ssn→Ename with PK {Ssn,Pnumber}\{\textsf{Ssn},\textsf{Pnumber}\}{Ssn,Pnumber}.
    • 3NF: 2NF, and no non-prime attribute is transitively dependent on the primary key. Example: EMP_DEPT is not 3NF since Ssn→Dnumber→Dname\textsf{Ssn}\to \textsf{Dnumber}\to \textsf{Dname}Ssn→Dnumber→Dname.

    General definitions and the differences

    Primary-key versionGeneral version
    Keys consideredonly the chosen PKall candidate keys
    Prime attributeattribute of the PK (in effect)attribute of any candidate key
    2NFnon-prime attributes fully dependent on the PKno non-prime attribute partially dependent on any key
    3NF2NF and no non-prime attribute transitively dependent on the PKfor every non-trivial X→AX \rightarrow AX→A: XXX is a superkey or AAA is prime (implies 2NF; test directly)

    The general versions catch partial and transitive dependencies on secondary keys. In LOTS (keys Property_id# and {County_name, Lot#}), County_name→Tax_rate\textsf{County\_name} \rightarrow \textsf{Tax\_rate}County_name→Tax_rate is a partial dependency on the second key: LOTS passes PK-based 2NF (PK Property_id# is a single attribute) but fails general 2NF. Conversely, since “prime” now includes attributes of all keys, an FD whose RHS is part of another key no longer counts against 3NF.

    Answer

    PK-based: 1NF atomic values; 2NF no partial dependency on the PK; 3NF additionally no transitive dependency on the PK. The general definitions apply the same ideas to every candidate key and use “prime = in some candidate key”; general 3NF is the single test “every non-trivial X→AX \rightarrow AX→A has XXX a superkey or AAA prime”.

    14.9What 2NF avoidsE&N Ex. 14.9 · p. 497

    What undesirable dependencies are avoided when a relation is in 2NF?

    Solution · written for this guide

    Partial dependencies: a non-prime attribute functionally dependent on a proper subset of a candidate key. Such an attribute describes only part of the key, so its value is repeated for every tuple sharing that part. Example: in EMP_PROJ, Ssn→Ename\textsf{Ssn} \rightarrow \textsf{Ename}Ssn→Ename repeats Ename for each project of an employee and Pnumber→{Pname,Plocation}\textsf{Pnumber} \rightarrow \{\textsf{Pname},\textsf{Plocation}\}Pnumber→{Pname,Plocation} repeats project data for each worker (with the resulting anomalies). 2NF removes them by moving each such attribute into a relation with the key part it depends on: EP1(Ssn, Pnumber, Hours), EP2(Ssn, Ename), EP3(Pnumber, Pname, Plocation).

    Answer

    Partial dependencies of non-prime attributes on part of a (candidate) key.

    14.10What 3NF avoidsE&N Ex. 14.10 · p. 497

    What undesirable dependencies are avoided when a relation is in 3NF?

    Solution · written for this guide

    Transitive dependencies of non-prime attributes on a key: key →Z→A\to Z\to A→Z→A where ZZZ is not a superkey (typically a non-prime attribute or set) and AAA is non-prime. Equivalently, a non-key attribute determining another non-key attribute. Example: EMP_DEPT with Ssn→Dnumber→{Dname,Dmgr_ssn}\textsf{Ssn}\to \textsf{Dnumber}\to\{\textsf{Dname},\textsf{Dmgr\_ssn}\}Ssn→Dnumber→{Dname,Dmgr_ssn} repeats department data per employee; 3NF splits it into ED1(Ename, Ssn, Bdate, Address, Dnumber) and ED2(Dnumber, Dname, Dmgr_ssn). Under the general definition, 3NF also excludes partial dependencies (it implies 2NF): it forbids every non-trivial X→AX \rightarrow AX→A with XXX not a superkey and AAA non-prime.

    Answer

    Transitive dependencies (non-prime attributes determined by non-key attributes), and, by the general definition, partial dependencies as well.

    14.11How the general definitions extend beyond primary keysE&N Ex. 14.11 · p. 497

    In what way do the generalized definitions of 2NF and 3NF extend the definitions beyond primary keys?

    Solution · written for this guide
    1. All candidate keys are used, not just the primary key: partial and transitive dependencies are tested against every key.
    2. Prime means belonging to any candidate key, so the set of attributes that are “protected” changes.
    3. General 2NF: no non-prime attribute is partially dependent on any key.
    4. General 3NF: whenever a non-trivial X→AX \rightarrow AX→A holds, XXX is a superkey or AAA is prime. This one condition covers both partial and transitive dependencies, so 3NF can be tested directly without 2NF first.

    Example: LOTS(Property_id#, County_name, Lot#, Area, Price, Tax_rate) with second key {County_name, Lot#}. County_name→Tax_rate\textsf{County\_name} \rightarrow \textsf{Tax\_rate}County_name→Tax_rate is invisible to PK-based 2NF but is a partial dependency on {County_name, Lot#}; general 2NF catches it and splits off LOTS2(County_name, Tax_rate). Area→Price\textsf{Area} \rightarrow \textsf{Price}Area→Price then violates general 3NF (Area not a superkey, Price non-prime), giving LOTS1A and LOTS1B.

    Answer

    They replace “the primary key” by “every candidate key” (and prime by “in some candidate key”), and 3NF becomes a single test on all FDs: LHS a superkey or RHS prime.

    14.12BCNF vs. 3NFE&N Ex. 14.12 · p. 497

    Define Boyce-Codd normal form. How does it differ from 3NF? Why is it considered a stronger form of 3NF?

    Solution · written for this guide

    Definition

    RRR is in BCNF if whenever a non-trivial FD X→AX \rightarrow AX→A holds in RRR, XXX is a superkey of RRR.

    Difference

    3NF allows X→AX \rightarrow AX→A when XXX is a superkey or AAA is prime. BCNF drops the “or AAA is prime” clause. So a relation is in 3NF but not BCNF exactly when some X→AX \rightarrow AX→A holds with XXX not a superkey and AAA prime.

    Why stronger

    Every BCNF relation satisfies 3NF (clause (a) alone is enough), but not conversely. Example: TEACH(Student, Course, Instructor) with {Student,Course}→Instructor\{\textsf{Student},\textsf{Course}\} \rightarrow \textsf{Instructor}{Student,Course}→Instructor and Instructor→Course\textsf{Instructor} \rightarrow \textsf{Course}Instructor→Course. Keys: {Student, Course} and {Student, Instructor} (since {S,I}+=SIC\{S,I\}^+=SIC{S,I}+=SIC), so every attribute is prime. Instructor→Course\textsf{Instructor} \rightarrow \textsf{Course}Instructor→Course is allowed by 3NF (Course is prime) but violates BCNF (Instructor+^++ = {Instructor, Course}, not a superkey). The redundancy is real: “Mark teaches Database” repeats for each of Mark’s students. The lossless BCNF decomposition is TEACH1(Instructor, Course), TEACH2(Student, Instructor) (common attribute Instructor is a key of TEACH1), but it loses {Student,Course}→Instructor\{\textsf{Student},\textsf{Course}\} \rightarrow \textsf{Instructor}{Student,Course}→Instructor; 3NF can always be reached with dependency preservation, BCNF cannot.

    Answer

    BCNF: every non-trivial FD’s LHS is a superkey. It is 3NF without the exception for prime right-hand sides, so BCNF ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ 3NF but not conversely (TEACH is 3NF, not BCNF); it removes all FD-based redundancy, at the possible cost of losing a dependency.

    8  Chapter 14 problems

    Textbook exercises

    Conventions used in every solution below
    • The given FDs are the whole story. The FDs that hold are exactly those in F+F^+F+ (everything derivable from the given ones). Keys and normal forms are judged from F+F^+F+, never from sample data.
    • Attributes are atomic, so every schema is in 1NF unless the question says otherwise.
    • Left-hand sides are non-empty (an FD ∅→A\emptyset\to A∅→A would make AAA constant).
    • Closure algorithm. Start with X+:=XX^+ := XX+:=X; whenever an FD Y→ZY\to ZY→Z has Y⊆X+Y\subseteq X^+Y⊆X+, add ZZZ; stop when a full pass adds nothing. In the tables, “→Y→Z\xrightarrow{Y\to Z}Y→Z​” shows the order in which FDs fire.
    • Key-finding shortcut. An attribute on no right-hand side is in every key; an attribute on right-hand sides only (never on a left) is in no key. Search only the “middle” ones.
    • Splitting rule. If X→YX\to YX→Y violates the target NF in RiR_iRi​, replace RiR_iRi​ by X∪YX\cup YX∪Y and Ri−(Y−X)R_i-(Y-X)Ri​−(Y−X). The common attributes are XXX, a key of X∪YX\cup YX∪Y, so every such split is lossless.
    14.19University transcript database: FDs and 3NF/BCNF designE&N Ex. 14.19 · p. 497

    Suppose that we have the following requirements for a university database that is used to keep track of students’ transcripts:

    1. The university keeps track of each student’s name (Sname), student number (Snum), Social Security number (Ssn), current address (Sc_addr) and phone (Sc_phone), permanent address (Sp_addr) and phone (Sp_phone), birth date (Bdate), sex (Sex), class (Class) (‘freshman’, ‘sophomore’, …, ‘graduate’), major department (Major_code), minor department (Minor_code) (if any), and degree program (Prog) (‘b.a.’, ‘b.s.’, …, ‘ph.d.’). Both Ssn and student number have unique values for each student.
    2. Each department is described by a name (Dname), department code (Dcode), office number (Doffice), office phone (Dphone), and college (Dcollege). Both name and code have unique values for each department.
    3. Each course has a course name (Cname), description (Cdesc), course number (Cnum), number of semester hours (Credit), level (Level), and offering department (Cdept). The course number is unique for each course.
    4. Each section has an instructor (Iname), semester (Semester), year (Year), course (Sec_course), and section number (Sec_num). The section number distinguishes different sections of the same course that are taught during the same semester/year; its values are 1, 2, 3, …, up to the total number of sections taught during each semester.
    5. A grade record refers to a student (Ssn), a particular section, and a grade (Grade).

    Design a relational database schema for this database application. First show all the functional dependencies that should hold among the attributes. Then design relation schemas for the database that are each in 3NF or BCNF. Specify the key attributes of each relation. Note any unspecified requirements, and make appropriate assumptions to render the specification complete.

    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. Each section has exactly one instructor, and Iname identifies the instructor. Why: the text says “each section has an instructor”; if team teaching were allowed, Iname would be multivalued and would need its own relation (SECTION_INSTR).
    2. A section is identified by (Sec_course, Semester, Year, Sec_num). Why: Sec_num restarts at 1 for each course in each semester/year, so it is unique only within that combination.
    3. Major_code, Minor_code and Cdept hold department codes. Why: the names end in “code”; we take Cdept to be a code too, so all three are foreign keys to Dcode.
    4. A student has one grade per section taken. Why: “a grade record refers to a student, a particular section, and a grade”.
    5. No other FDs hold: e.g. Doffice does not determine Dphone, an address does not determine a phone, two departments may share an office building, two courses may share a name. Why: nothing in the requirements forces them; adding them would create extra 3NF violations.
    6. The current and permanent address/phone are single atomic values (no 1NF issue).

    Step 1: functional dependencies

    • FD1 Ssn →\to→ {Snum, Sname, Sc_addr, Sc_phone, Sp_addr, Sp_phone, Bdate, Sex, Class, Major_code, Minor_code, Prog}
    • FD2 Snum→Ssn\text{\textsf{Snum}} \rightarrow \text{\textsf{Ssn}}Snum→Ssn   (so Snum also determines every student attribute)
    • FD3 Dcode→{Dname, Doffice, Dphone, Dcollege}\text{\textsf{Dcode}} \rightarrow \{\text{\textsf{Dname, Doffice, Dphone, Dcollege}}\}Dcode→{Dname, Doffice, Dphone, Dcollege}
    • FD4 Dname→Dcode\text{\textsf{Dname}} \rightarrow \text{\textsf{Dcode}}Dname→Dcode   (both are unique)
    • FD5 Cnum→{Cname, Cdesc, Credit, Level, Cdept}\text{\textsf{Cnum}} \rightarrow \{\text{\textsf{Cname, Cdesc, Credit, Level, Cdept}}\}Cnum→{Cname, Cdesc, Credit, Level, Cdept}
    • FD6 {Sec_course, Semester, Year, Sec_num}→Iname\{\text{\textsf{Sec\_course, Semester, Year, Sec\_num}}\} \rightarrow \text{\textsf{Iname}}{Sec_course, Semester, Year, Sec_num}→Iname
    • FD7 {Ssn, Sec_course, Semester, Year, Sec_num}→Grade\{\text{\textsf{Ssn, Sec\_course, Semester, Year, Sec\_num}}\} \rightarrow \text{\textsf{Grade}}{Ssn, Sec_course, Semester, Year, Sec_num}→Grade

    Step 2: relations (one per group of FDs with the same determinant), keys, foreign keys

    • STUDENT(Ssn, Snum, Sname, Sc_addr, Sc_phone, Sp_addr, Sp_phone, Bdate, Sex, Class, Major_code, Minor_code, Prog)
      Candidate keys Ssn and Snum (Ssn+^++ = all by FD1; Snum+^++: FD2 gives Ssn, then FD1 gives all). Major_code → DEPARTMENT.Dcode, Minor_code → DEPARTMENT.Dcode (NULL allowed).
    • DEPARTMENT(Dcode, Dname, Doffice, Dphone, Dcollege); candidate keys Dcode, Dname.
    • COURSE(Cnum, Cname, Cdesc, Credit, Level, Cdept); key Cnum; Cdept → DEPARTMENT.Dcode.
    • SECTION(Sec_course, Semester, Year, Sec_num, Iname); Sec_course → COURSE.Cnum.
    • GRADE_REPORT(Ssn, Sec_course, Semester, Year, Sec_num, Grade); Ssn → STUDENT.Ssn; (Sec_course, Semester, Year, Sec_num) → SECTION.

    Step 3: normal-form check

    In every relation the only non-trivial FDs that hold (projecting FD1–FD7) have a candidate key on the left: FD1, FD2 in STUDENT; FD3, FD4 in DEPARTMENT; FD5 in COURSE; FD6 in SECTION; FD7 in GRADE_REPORT. So every relation is in BCNF (hence 3NF). FD2 and FD4 relate two candidate keys; they do not violate BCNF because their left side is itself a key. The decomposition is dependency-preserving (each FD lives in one relation) and lossless (each relation is linked through a key / foreign key).

    Answer

    Five relations STUDENT, DEPARTMENT, COURSE, SECTION, GRADE_REPORT as above, all in BCNF, with keys {Ssn, Snum}, {Dcode, Dname}, Cnum, (Sec_course, Semester, Year, Sec_num) and (Ssn, Sec_course, Semester, Year, Sec_num).

    Valid alternatives. Many students have no minor, so Minor_code is often NULL; by Guideline 3 one may move it to STUDENT_MINOR(Ssn, Minor_code). A surrogate Section_id may replace the 4-attribute section key (then {Sec_course, Semester, Year, Sec_num} stays a second candidate key, declared UNIQUE).

    What the grader checks

    Every FD written explicitly, including the “both unique” ones (Snum→Ssn\text{Snum} \rightarrow \text{Ssn}Snum→Ssn, Dname→Dcode\text{Dname} \rightarrow \text{Dcode}Dname→Dcode); the composite section key (Sec_num alone is not a key); every relation’s key stated and every FK named; a sentence justifying BCNF/3NF for each relation; unstated requirements (instructor per section, minor optional, Cdept as code) written as assumptions with reasons.
