    Exam technique

    For “what anomalies” questions, give one concrete tuple-level example per anomaly type and name the FD that causes it; this links the informal guideline to the formal NF.

    14.21Normal form of LOTS: primary-key vs general definitionsE&N Ex. 14.21 · p. 498

    In what normal form is the LOTS relation schema in Figure 14.12(a) with respect to the restrictive interpretations of normal form that take only the primary key into account? Would it be in the same normal form if the general definitions of normal form were used?

    Figure 14.12(a): LOTS(Property_id#, County_name, Lot#, Area, Price, Tax_rate) with candidate keys Property_id# (primary) and {County_name, Lot#}:
    FD1 Property_id#→{County_name, Lot#, Area, Price, Tax_rate}\text{\textsf{Property\_id\#}} \rightarrow \{\text{\textsf{County\_name, Lot\#, Area, Price, Tax\_rate}}\}Property_id#→{County_name, Lot#, Area, Price, Tax_rate};
    FD2 {County_name, Lot#}→{Property_id#, Area, Price, Tax_rate}\{\text{\textsf{County\_name, Lot\#}}\} \rightarrow \{\text{\textsf{Property\_id\#, Area, Price, Tax\_rate}}\}{County_name, Lot#}→{Property_id#, Area, Price, Tax_rate};
    FD3 County_name→Tax_rate\text{\textsf{County\_name}} \rightarrow \text{\textsf{Tax\_rate}}County_name→Tax_rate; FD4 Area→Price\text{\textsf{Area}} \rightarrow \text{\textsf{Price}}Area→Price.

    Solution · written for this guide

    Keys (checked by closure)

    {Property_id#}+\{\text{Property\_id\#}\}^{+}{Property_id#}+ = all attributes by FD1. {County_name, Lot#}+\{\text{County\_name, Lot\#}\}^{+}{County_name, Lot#}+ = all by FD2; it is minimal since {County_name}+\{\text{County\_name}\}^{+}{County_name}+ ={=\{={County_name, Tax_rate}\}} and {Lot#}+\{\text{Lot\#}\}^{+}{Lot#}+ ={=\{={Lot#}\}}. No other key exists (verified exhaustively). Prime attributes (general view): Property_id#, County_name, Lot#.

    (a) Primary-key-only definitions (primary key = Property_id#)

    • 1NF: attributes atomic. Yes.
    • 2NF: the primary key is a single attribute, so no attribute can depend on a part of it. Yes.
    • 3NF: with only the primary key considered, County_name and Area are non-key attributes, and FD3 and FD4 make Tax_rate and Price transitively dependent on the key: Property_id# →\to→ County_name →\to→ Tax_rate and Property_id# →\to→ Area →\to→ Price. No.

    So LOTS is in 2NF.

    (b) General definitions (all candidate keys)

    FD3 County_name→Tax_rate\text{County\_name} \rightarrow \text{Tax\_rate}County_name→Tax_rate: County_name is a proper subset of the candidate key {County_name, Lot#} and Tax_rate is non-prime, so Tax_rate is partially dependent on a key: the general 2NF definition is violated. Hence LOTS is only in 1NF. (FD4 additionally violates 3NF: Area is not a superkey and Price is non-prime.)

    Answer

    2NF under the primary-key-only definitions; only 1NF under the general definitions, because FD3 is a partial dependency on the second candidate key {County_name, Lot#}. So the answer is not the same.

    Watch out

    Saying “Property_id# is a single-attribute key, so LOTS is in 2NF” under the general definition. The general 2NF must be checked against every candidate key.

    14.22Every two-attribute schema is in BCNFE&N Ex. 14.22 · p. 498

    Prove that any relation schema with two attributes is in BCNF.

    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. Left-hand sides of FDs are non-empty. Why: with ∅→A\emptyset\to A∅→A allowed, R(A,B)R(A,B)R(A,B) with only ∅→A\emptyset\to A∅→A would violate BCNF (∅\emptyset∅ is not a superkey), so the statement needs this standard convention.

    Let R={A,B}R=\{A,B\}R={A,B} and let X→YX \rightarrow YX→Y be any non-trivial FD in F+F^+F+, i.e. Y⊈XY\not\subseteq XY⊆X.

    1. X≠∅X\neq\emptysetX=∅ (assumption) and X≠RX\neq RX=R (if X={A,B}X=\{A,B\}X={A,B}, every Y⊆RY\subseteq RY⊆R is inside XXX, so the FD would be trivial). Hence XXX is a single attribute; say X={A}X=\{A\}X={A} (the case X={B}X=\{B\}X={B} is symmetric).
    2. Non-trivial means YYY contains an attribute outside XXX; the only one is BBB. So A→BA \rightarrow BA→B holds.
    3. Then {A}+⊇{A,B}=R\{A\}^+\supseteq\{A,B\}=R{A}+⊇{A,B}=R, so X={A}X=\{A\}X={A} is a superkey.

    Every non-trivial FD has a superkey on its left, which is exactly the BCNF definition.

    Check by cases (all four possibilities): no FD (key ABABAB, nothing to check); only A→BA \rightarrow BA→B (key AAA); only B→AB \rightarrow AB→A (key BBB); both (keys AAA and BBB). In each case every non-trivial FD has a key on the left.

    Answer

    Any non-trivial FD on a two-attribute schema has the form A→BA \rightarrow BA→B (or B→AB \rightarrow AB→A), whose left side is then a key; so the BCNF condition always holds.

    14.23Why the join of EMP_PROJ1 and EMP_LOCS gives spurious tuplesE&N Ex. 14.23 · p. 498

    Why do spurious tuples occur in the result of joining the EMP_PROJ1 and EMP_LOCS relations in Figure 14.5 (result shown in Figure 14.6)?

    Figure 14.5: EMP_LOCS(Ename, Plocation) and EMP_PROJ1(Ssn, Pnumber, Hours, Pname, Plocation), the projections of the EMP_PROJ state of Figure 14.4 (Exercise 14.20). Figure 14.6 shows their NATURAL JOIN (on Plocation), with the spurious tuples starred.

    Solution · written for this guide

    The reason

    The natural join matches on the only common attribute, Plocation, which is neither a key nor a foreign key in either relation. A location such as Houston is shared by several projects (3 and 20) and by several employees (Narayan, Wong, Wallace, Borg), so every EMP_PROJ1 tuple in Houston joins with every employee who works on some Houston project. Those combinations were never in EMP_PROJ.

    Example: (123456789, 1, 32.5, ProductX, Bellaire) joins with (English, Joyce A., Bellaire), producing a tuple saying English is employee 123456789 on ProductX; it is spurious.

    Formal view: the decomposition is lossy

    A binary decomposition {R1,R2}\{R_1,R_2\}{R1​,R2​} is lossless iff (R1∩R2)→(R1−R2)(R_1\cap R_2)\to(R_1-R_2)(R1​∩R2​)→(R1​−R2​) or (R1∩R2)→(R2−R1)(R_1\cap R_2)\to(R_2-R_1)(R1​∩R2​)→(R2​−R1​) is in F+F^+F+. Here R1∩R2={Plocation}R_1\cap R_2=\{\text{Plocation}\}R1​∩R2​={Plocation}, and neither Plocation→Ename\text{Plocation} \rightarrow \text{Ename}Plocation→Ename nor Plocation→{Ssn, Pnumber, Hours, Pname}\text{Plocation} \rightarrow \{\text{Ssn, Pnumber, Hours, Pname}\}Plocation→{Ssn, Pnumber, Hours, Pname} holds (the instance already contradicts both: Bellaire →\to→ Smith and English; Houston →\to→ projects 3 and 20). So the test fails.

    On the full Figure 14.4 state the join returns 57 tuples instead of 16, so 41 are spurious (computed); for Ssn 123456789 alone it returns 5 tuples, 3 spurious, as in Figure 14.6.

    Answer

    Because the relations are joined on Plocation, which is not a (primary key, foreign key) pair: Plocation determines neither side, so the decomposition of EMP_PROJ into EMP_PROJ1 and EMP_LOCS fails the lossless (non-additive) join test and the join manufactures tuples (violating Guideline 4).

    14.24Key of R; decompose into 2NF and then 3NFE&N Ex. 14.24 · p. 498★ Must-do

    Consider the universal relation R={A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H,I,J}R=\{A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H,I,J\}R={A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H,I,J} and the set of functional dependencies F={{A,B}→{C}, {A}→{D,E}, {B}→{F}, {F}→{G,H}, {D}→{I,J}}F=\{\{A,B\} \rightarrow \{C\},\ \{A\} \rightarrow \{D,E\},\ \{B\} \rightarrow \{F\},\ \{F\} \rightarrow \{G,H\},\ \{D\} \rightarrow \{I,J\}\}F={{A,B}→{C}, {A}→{D,E}, {B}→{F}, {F}→{G,H}, {D}→{I,J}}. What is the key for RRR? Decompose RRR into 2NF and then 3NF relations.

    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. FFF is the complete set of FDs; attributes are atomic (so RRR is in 1NF). Why: the question gives no other information; keys/NFs are judged from F+F^+F+.

    Step 1: closures (FDs in firing order)

    Step 2: the key

    AAA and BBB appear on no right-hand side, so both are in every key. {A,B}+=R\{A,B\}^+=R{A,B}+=R, so ABABAB is a superkey; it is minimal because A+=ADEIJ≠RA^+=ADEIJ\neq RA+=ADEIJ=R and B+=BFGH≠RB^+=BFGH\neq RB+=BFGH=R. Hence {A,B}\{A,B\}{A,B} is the only candidate key. Prime: A,BA,BA,B. Non-prime: C,D,E,F,G,H,I,JC,D,E,F,G,H,I,JC,D,E,F,G,H,I,J.

    Step 3: normal form of RRR

    2NF fails: A→DEA \rightarrow DEA→DE with A⊂ABA\subset ABA⊂AB and D,ED,ED,E non-prime (partial dependency); likewise B→FB \rightarrow FB→F (and the derived A→IJA \rightarrow IJA→IJ, B→GHB \rightarrow GHB→GH). So RRR is in 1NF only.

    Step 4: decompose into 2NF (remove partial dependencies)

    Put each non-prime attribute with the smallest part of the key it depends on, using the closures:

    1. Split RRR on A→DEIJA \rightarrow DEIJA→DEIJ (=A+−A=A^+-A=A+−A): R2(A,D,E,I,J)R_2(A,D,E,I,J)R2​(A,D,E,I,J) and R−{D,E,I,J}=(A,B,C,F,G,H)R-\{D,E,I,J\}=(A,B,C,F,G,H)R−{D,E,I,J}=(A,B,C,F,G,H). Common attribute AAA is the key of R2R_2R2​: lossless.
    2. Split (A,B,C,F,G,H)(A,B,C,F,G,H)(A,B,C,F,G,H) on B→FGHB \rightarrow FGHB→FGH: R3(B,F,G,H)R_3(B,F,G,H)R3​(B,F,G,H) and R1(A,B,C)R_1(A,B,C)R1​(A,B,C). Common BBB is the key of R3R_3R3​.
    RelationFDs holding (projected)KeyNF
    R1(A,B,C)R_1(A,B,C)R1​(A,B,C)AB→CAB \rightarrow CAB→CABABABBCNF
    R2(A,D,E,I,J)R_2(A,D,E,I,J)R2​(A,D,E,I,J)A→DEA \rightarrow DEA→DE, D→IJD \rightarrow IJD→IJ (so A→IJA \rightarrow IJA→IJ)AAA2NF, not 3NF (D→IJD \rightarrow IJD→IJ)
    R3(B,F,G,H)R_3(B,F,G,H)R3​(B,F,G,H)B→FB \rightarrow FB→F, F→GHF \rightarrow GHF→GH (so B→GHB \rightarrow GHB→GH)BBB2NF, not 3NF (F→GHF \rightarrow GHF→GH)

    R2R_2R2​, R3R_3R3​ have single-attribute keys, so no partial dependency is possible: all three are in 2NF.

    Step 5: decompose into 3NF (remove transitive dependencies)

    1. R2R_2R2​: D→IJD \rightarrow IJD→IJ, DDD not a superkey of R2R_2R2​, I,JI,JI,J non-prime. Split into R21(D,I,J)R_{21}(D,I,J)R21​(D,I,J) (key DDD) and R22(A,D,E)R_{22}(A,D,E)R22​(A,D,E) (key AAA, A→DEA \rightarrow DEA→DE). Common DDD is the key of R21R_{21}R21​.
    2. R3R_3R3​: F→GHF \rightarrow GHF→GH, FFF not a superkey of R3R_3R3​. Split into R31(F,G,H)R_{31}(F,G,H)R31​(F,G,H) (key FFF) and R32(B,F)R_{32}(B,F)R32​(B,F) (key BBB, B→FB \rightarrow FB→F). Common FFF is the key of R31R_{31}R31​.
    Answer

    Key: {A,B}\{A,B\}{A,B}.   2NF: R1(A,B‾,C)R_1(\underline{A,B},C)R1​(A,B​,C), R2(A‾,D,E,I,J)R_2(\underline{A},D,E,I,J)R2​(A​,D,E,I,J), R3(B‾,F,G,H)R_3(\underline{B},F,G,H)R3​(B​,F,G,H).   3NF: R1(A,B‾,C)R_1(\underline{A,B},C)R1​(A,B​,C), R22(A‾,D,E)R_{22}(\underline{A},D,E)R22​(A​,D,E), R21(D‾,I,J)R_{21}(\underline{D},I,J)R21​(D​,I,J), R32(B‾,F)R_{32}(\underline{B},F)R32​(B​,F), R31(F‾,G,H)R_{31}(\underline{F},G,H)R31​(F​,G,H). Each 3NF relation has a single FD whose left side is its key, so each is in fact in BCNF.

    Lossless: every split’s common attributes were a key of one side (chase on the final five relations also gives an all-aaa row). Dependency-preserving: each of the five given FDs lies inside one final relation.

    What the grader checks

    Closures with steps (1); key ABABAB with minimality shown, not just “superkey” (1); prime/non-prime listed; 2NF violation named with reason (A→DEA \rightarrow DEA→DE: part of key, non-prime). Each split names its FD and lists the FDs holding in each part; 0 for the final-answer mark if any final relation is not in 3NF (e.g. leaving (A,D,E,I,J)(A,D,E,I,J)(A,D,E,I,J)). Putting I,JI,JI,J with ABABAB or with AAA inside the 3NF answer loses marks: they depend on DDD. Error carried forward from a wrong key.

    Repeat Exercise 14.24 for the following different set of functional dependencies G={{A,B}→{C}, {B,D}→{E,F}, {A,D}→{G,H}, {A}→{I}, {H}→{J}}G=\{\{A,B\} \rightarrow \{C\},\ \{B,D\} \rightarrow \{E,F\},\ \{A,D\} \rightarrow \{G,H\},\ \{A\} \rightarrow \{I\},\ \{H\} \rightarrow \{J\}\}G={{A,B}→{C}, {B,D}→{E,F}, {A,D}→{G,H}, {A}→{I}, {H}→{J}}.

    Step 2: the key

    AAA, BBB, DDD appear on no right-hand side, so every key contains ABDABDABD. Since {A,B,D}+=R\{A,B,D\}^+=R{A,B,D}+=R, ABDABDABD is a superkey, and it is minimal because its 2-subsets have closures ABCIABCIABCI, ADGHIJADGHIJADGHIJ, BDEFBDEFBDEF, none equal to RRR. So {A,B,D}\{A,B,D\}{A,B,D} is the only candidate key. Prime: A,B,DA,B,DA,B,D; non-prime: C,E,F,G,H,I,JC,E,F,G,H,I,JC,E,F,G,H,I,J.

    Step 3: normal form of RRR

    Every one of AB→CAB \rightarrow CAB→C, BD→EFBD \rightarrow EFBD→EF, AD→GHAD \rightarrow GHAD→GH, A→IA \rightarrow IA→I has a proper subset of the key on the left and a non-prime right side: partial dependencies, so RRR is in 1NF only.

    Step 4: 2NF decomposition (one split per partial dependency)

    Using the closures, each non-prime attribute goes with the smallest key part that determines it (III depends on AAA alone even though AB→CIAB \rightarrow CIAB→CI; JJJ follows ADADAD via HHH).

    1. Split on A→IA \rightarrow IA→I: (A,I)(A,I)(A,I) and (A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H,J)(A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H,J)(A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H,J); common AAA = key of (A,I)(A,I)(A,I).
    2. Split the rest on AB→CAB \rightarrow CAB→C: (A,B,C)(A,B,C)(A,B,C) and (A,B,D,E,F,G,H,J)(A,B,D,E,F,G,H,J)(A,B,D,E,F,G,H,J); common ABABAB = key of (A,B,C)(A,B,C)(A,B,C).
    3. Split the rest on BD→EFBD \rightarrow EFBD→EF: (B,D,E,F)(B,D,E,F)(B,D,E,F) and (A,B,D,G,H,J)(A,B,D,G,H,J)(A,B,D,G,H,J); common BDBDBD = key of (B,D,E,F)(B,D,E,F)(B,D,E,F).
    4. Split the rest on AD→GHJAD \rightarrow GHJAD→GHJ: (A,D,G,H,J)(A,D,G,H,J)(A,D,G,H,J) and (A,B,D)(A,B,D)(A,B,D); common ADADAD = key of (A,D,G,H,J)(A,D,G,H,J)(A,D,G,H,J).
    RelationFDs holdingKeyNF
    R1(A,B,C)R_1(A,B,C)R1​(A,B,C)AB→CAB \rightarrow CAB→CABABABBCNF
    R2(B,D,E,F)R_2(B,D,E,F)R2​(B,D,E,F)BD→EFBD \rightarrow EFBD→EFBDBDBDBCNF
    R3(A,D,G,H,J)R_3(A,D,G,H,J)R3​(A,D,G,H,J)AD→GHAD \rightarrow GHAD→GH, H→JH \rightarrow JH→J (so AD→JAD \rightarrow JAD→J)ADADAD2NF, not 3NF (H→JH \rightarrow JH→J)
    R4(A,I)R_4(A,I)R4​(A,I)A→IA \rightarrow IA→IAAABCNF
    R5(A,B,D)R_5(A,B,D)R5​(A,B,D)none (all-key)ABDABDABDBCNF

    Step 5: 3NF

    Only R3R_3R3​ violates 3NF: H→JH \rightarrow JH→J, HHH is not a superkey of R3R_3R3​ and JJJ is non-prime (transitive AD→H→JAD\to H\to JAD→H→J). Split into R31(H,J)R_{31}(H,J)R31​(H,J) (key HHH) and R32(A,D,G,H)R_{32}(A,D,G,H)R32​(A,D,G,H) (key ADADAD, AD→GHAD \rightarrow GHAD→GH); common HHH = key of R31R_{31}R31​.

    Answer

    Key: {A,B,D}\{A,B,D\}{A,B,D}.   2NF: R1(A,B‾,C)R_1(\underline{A,B},C)R1​(A,B​,C), R2(B,D‾,E,F)R_2(\underline{B,D},E,F)R2​(B,D​,E,F), R3(A,D‾,G,H,J)R_3(\underline{A,D},G,H,J)R3​(A,D​,G,H,J), R4(A‾,I)R_4(\underline{A},I)R4​(A​,I), R5(A,B,D‾)R_5(\underline{A,B,D})R5​(A,B,D​).   3NF: R1(A,B‾,C)R_1(\underline{A,B},C)R1​(A,B​,C), R2(B,D‾,E,F)R_2(\underline{B,D},E,F)R2​(B,D​,E,F), R32(A,D‾,G,H)R_{32}(\underline{A,D},G,H)R32​(A,D​,G,H), R31(H‾,J)R_{31}(\underline{H},J)R31​(H​,J), R4(A‾,I)R_4(\underline{A},I)R4​(A​,I), R5(A,B,D‾)R_5(\underline{A,B,D})R5​(A,B,D​) (all in BCNF).

    Lossless: each split shares a key of one side; chase on the six final relations confirms it. Dependency-preserving: each of the five FDs of GGG lies in one relation.

    Watch out

    Dropping R5(A,B,D)R_5(A,B,D)R5​(A,B,D). Without a relation containing the key ABDABDABD the decomposition is lossy (R1∩R2={B}R_1\cap R_2=\{B\}R1​∩R2​={B} etc. determine nothing): the rubric gives 0 for a lossy answer.

    What the grader checks

    Same scheme as 14.24; 0 for the final mark if lossy (no relation containing ABDABDABD) or if (A,D,G,H,J)(A,D,G,H,J)(A,D,G,H,J) is left in the 3NF answer.

    14.26Which FDs may hold in a given relation stateE&N Ex. 14.26 · p. 498

    Consider the following relation:

    ABCTUPLE#
    10b1c11
    10b2c22
    11b4c13
    12b3c44
    13b1c15
    14b3c46
    1. Given the previous extension (state), which of the following dependencies may hold in the above relation? If the dependency cannot hold, explain why by specifying the tuples that cause the violation.   i. A→BA\to BA→B, ii. B→CB\to CB→C, iii. C→BC\to BC→B, iv. B→AB\to AB→A, v. C→AC\to AC→A
    2. Does the above relation have a potential candidate key? If it does, what is it? If it does not, why not?
    Solution · written for this guide
    What an instance can and cannot tell you

    An FD is a constraint on all legal states. One state can disprove X→YX \rightarrow YX→Y (two tuples agree on XXX but differ on YYY), but it can never prove it. So the right answer is “may hold” (consistent with this state), not “holds”.

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. TUPLE# is only a label for the rows and is not an attribute of the relation. Why: otherwise it would trivially be a key and the question would be pointless.

    Step 1: group the tuples on each left-hand side (all 15 pairs checked)

    Only pairs that agree on the left side can violate an FD.

    LHSPairs of tuples agreeing on LHSOther pairs
    AAA(1,2): A=10A=10A=10all others differ on AAA
    BBB(1,5): B=b1B=b1B=b1; (4,6): B=b3B=b3B=b3all others differ on BBB
    CCC(1,3), (1,5), (3,5): C=c1C=c1C=c1; (4,6): C=c4C=c4C=c4all others differ on CCC

    Step 2: test each FD on those pairs

    FDCheck of agreeing pairsVerdict
    i. A→BA \rightarrow BA→B(1,2): BBB = b1 vs b2cannot hold (tuples 1, 2)
    ii. B→CB \rightarrow CB→C(1,5): c1 = c1 ✓; (4,6): c4 = c4 ✓may hold
    iii. C→BC \rightarrow BC→B(1,3): b1 vs b4 ×\times×; (3,5): b4 vs b1 ×\times×; (1,5), (4,6) agreecannot hold (tuples 1, 3 or 3, 5)
    iv. B→AB \rightarrow AB→A(1,5): 10 vs 13 ×\times×; (4,6): 12 vs 14 ×\times×cannot hold (1, 5 or 4, 6)
    v. C→AC \rightarrow AC→A(1,3): 10 vs 11; (1,5): 10 vs 13; (3,5): 11 vs 13; (4,6): 12 vs 14cannot hold (e.g. 1, 3)

    Step 3 (b): potential candidate keys

    A candidate key must at least have distinct values in every tuple of this state.

    • Single attributes: AAA repeats (tuples 1, 2), BBB repeats (1, 5), CCC repeats (1, 3). None is unique.
    • Pairs: {A,B}\{A,B\}{A,B} unique ✓; {A,C}\{A,C\}{A,C} unique ✓; {B,C}\{B,C\}{B,C} repeats (tuples 4, 6: (b3, c4)) ×\times×.

    So {A,B}\{A,B\}{A,B} and {A,C}\{A,C\}{A,C} are unique in this state and minimal (no single attribute is unique). Also, of all FDs with one- or two-attribute left side, the only non-trivial ones consistent with the state are B→CB \rightarrow CB→C, AB→CAB \rightarrow CAB→C, AC→BAC \rightarrow BAC→B, matching these two keys.

    Answer

    (a) Only B→CB \rightarrow CB→C may hold. A→BA \rightarrow BA→B is violated by tuples 1, 2; C→BC \rightarrow BC→B by 1, 3; B→AB \rightarrow AB→A by 1, 5; C→AC \rightarrow AC→A by 1, 3.   (b) Yes: {A,B}\{A,B\}{A,B} and {A,C}\{A,C\}{A,C} are potential candidate keys (each is unique in this state and minimal). Whether they really are keys depends on the semantics of all legal states, which one instance cannot establish.

    Watch out

    Writing “B→CB \rightarrow CB→C holds”. The instance only shows it is not violated. Likewise for keys: say “potential”/“consistent with the state”.

    14.27Is ABABAB a candidate key? Is ABDABDABD?E&N Ex. 14.27 · p. 499★ Must-do

    Consider a relation R(A,B,C,D,E)R(A,B,C,D,E)R(A,B,C,D,E) with the following dependencies:

    AB→C,CD→E,DE→B.AB \rightarrow C,\qquad CD \rightarrow E,\qquad DE \rightarrow B.AB→C,CD→E,DE→B.

    Is ABABAB a candidate key of this relation? If not, is ABDABDABD? Explain your answer.

    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. The three FDs are the complete set; a candidate key is a minimal superkey (X+=RX^+=RX+=R and no proper subset has this property).

    Step 1: is ABABAB a key?

    {A,B}+\{A,B\}^+{A,B}+: AB→AB→CABCAB\xrightarrow{AB\to C}ABCABAB→C​ABC. Now CD→ECD \rightarrow ECD→E needs DDD and DE→BDE \rightarrow BDE→B needs D,ED,ED,E: nothing more fires. {A,B}+={A,B,C}≠R\{A,B\}^+=\{A,B,C\}\neq R{A,B}+={A,B,C}=R (DDD, EEE missing). ABABAB is not a superkey, so not a candidate key.

    Step 2: is ABDABDABD a key?

    Superkey: ABD→AB→CABCD→CD→EABCDE=RABD\xrightarrow{AB\to C}ABCD\xrightarrow{CD\to E}ABCDE=RABDAB→C​ABCDCD→E​ABCDE=R. ✓

    Minimality: check every proper subset of size 2 (subsets of those are smaller still):

    SubsetClosureSuperkey?
    ABABABABCABCABC (Step 1)no
    ADADADADADAD (no left side ⊆AD\subseteq AD⊆AD)no
    BDBDBDBDBDBD (no left side ⊆BD\subseteq BD⊆BD)no

    No proper subset is a superkey, so ABDABDABD is a candidate key.

    Going further: all keys and the normal form

    AAA and DDD are on no right-hand side, so every key contains ADADAD; {A,D}+=AD\{A,D\}^+=AD{A,D}+=AD, so add one more attribute: ABDABDABD (above), ACD→CD→EACDE→DE→BRACD\xrightarrow{CD\to E}ACDE\xrightarrow{DE\to B}RACDCD→E​ACDEDE→B​R, ADE→DE→BABDE→AB→CRADE\xrightarrow{DE\to B}ABDE \xrightarrow{AB\to C}RADEDE→B​ABDEAB→C​R. All three are minimal (their 2-subsets other than ADADAD are not superkeys either). Candidate keys: ABDABDABD, ACDACDACD, ADEADEADE (checked exhaustively by program). Every attribute is prime, so RRR is in 3NF; it is not in BCNF since e.g. AB→CAB \rightarrow CAB→C has a non-superkey left side.

    Answer

    ABABAB is not a candidate key ({A,B}+={A,B,C}≠R\{A,B\}^+=\{A,B,C\}\neq R{A,B}+={A,B,C}=R). ABDABDABD is a candidate key: {A,B,D}+=R\{A,B,D\}^+=R{A,B,D}+=R and none of ABABAB, ADADAD, BDBDBD is a superkey. (The other keys are ACDACDACD and ADEADEADE.)

    What the grader checks

    Closure of ABABAB shown with steps (0.5 if only asserted); closure of ABDABDABD shown; minimality of ABDABDABD shown by checking its proper subsets (0 for this part if the answer stops at “superkey”).

    14.28Course/section schedule relation: keys and normalizationE&N Ex. 14.28 · p. 499

    Consider the relation RRR, which has attributes that hold schedules of courses and sections at a university; R={R=\{R={Course_no, Sec_no, Offering_dept, Credit_hours, Course_level, Instructor_ssn, Semester, Year, Days_hours, Room_no, No_of_students}\}}. Suppose that the following functional dependencies hold on RRR:

    • {Course_no}→{Offering_dept, Credit_hours, Course_level}\{\text{\textsf{Course\_no}}\} \rightarrow \{\text{\textsf{Offering\_dept, Credit\_hours, Course\_level}}\}{Course_no}→{Offering_dept, Credit_hours, Course_level}
    • {Course_no, Sec_no, Semester, Year}→{Days_hours, Room_no, No_of_students, Instructor_ssn}\{\text{\textsf{Course\_no, Sec\_no, Semester, Year}}\} \rightarrow \{\text{\textsf{Days\_hours, Room\_no, No\_of\_students, Instructor\_ssn}}\}{Course_no, Sec_no, Semester, Year}→{Days_hours, Room_no, No_of_students, Instructor_ssn}
    • {Room_no, Days_hours, Semester, Year}→{Instructor_ssn, Course_no, Sec_no}\{\text{\textsf{Room\_no, Days\_hours, Semester, Year}}\} \rightarrow \{\text{\textsf{Instructor\_ssn, Course\_no, Sec\_no}}\}{Room_no, Days_hours, Semester, Year}→{Instructor_ssn, Course_no, Sec_no}

    Try to determine which sets of attributes form keys of RRR. How would you normalize this relation?

    Solution · written for this guide

    Abbreviations. CN = Course_no, SN = Sec_no, OD = Offering_dept, CH = Credit_hours, CL = Course_level, IS = Instructor_ssn, SE = Semester, YR = Year, DH = Days_hours, RN = Room_no, NS = No_of_students. FDs: FD1 CN→OD,CH,CL\text{CN} \rightarrow \text{OD,CH,CL}CN→OD,CH,CL; FD2 CN,SN,SE,YR→DH,RN,NS,IS\text{CN,SN,SE,YR} \rightarrow \text{DH,RN,NS,IS}CN,SN,SE,YR→DH,RN,NS,IS; FD3 RN,DH,SE,YR→IS,CN,SN\text{RN,DH,SE,YR} \rightarrow \text{IS,CN,SN}RN,DH,SE,YR→IS,CN,SN.

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. These three FDs are all the FDs. Why: given; e.g. we do not assume IS,DH,SE,YR→RN\text{IS,DH,SE,YR} \rightarrow \text{RN}IS,DH,SE,YR→RN (an instructor is in one room at a time) since it is not stated.
    2. Days_hours is one atomic value (e.g. “MWF 10–11”), so RRR is in 1NF.

    Step 1: classify attributes

    • On no right-hand side: SE, YR ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ in every key.
    • Only on right-hand sides: OD, CH, CL, NS, IS ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ in no key.
    • Both sides (“middle”): CN, SN, RN, DH. Keys are {SE,YR}∪\{SE,YR\}\cup{SE,YR}∪ some subset of these.

    Step 2: closures

    • {SE,YR}+={SE,YR}\{SE,YR\}^+=\{SE,YR\}{SE,YR}+={SE,YR}. Adding one middle attribute: {SE,YR,CN}+={SE,YR,CN,OD,CH,CL}\{SE,YR,CN\}^+=\{SE,YR,CN,OD,CH,CL\}{SE,YR,CN}+={SE,YR,CN,OD,CH,CL} (FD1); {SE,YR,SN}+\{SE,YR,SN\}^+{SE,YR,SN}+, {SE,YR,RN}+\{SE,YR,RN\}^+{SE,YR,RN}+, {SE,YR,DH}+\{SE,YR,DH\}^+{SE,YR,DH}+ add nothing. None is RRR.
    • {CN,SN,SE,YR}+\{CN,SN,SE,YR\}^+{CN,SN,SE,YR}+: →FD1\xrightarrow{FD1}FD1​ +OD, CH, CL →FD2\xrightarrow{FD2}FD2​ +DH, RN, NS, IS =R=R=R. ✓
    • {RN,DH,SE,YR}+\{RN,DH,SE,YR\}^+{RN,DH,SE,YR}+: →FD3\xrightarrow{FD3}FD3​ +IS, CN, SN →FD1\xrightarrow{FD1}FD1​ +OD, CH, CL →FD2\xrightarrow{FD2}FD2​ +NS =R=R=R. ✓
    • The other pairs of middle attributes with SE, YR: {CN,RN}: FD1 only; {CN,DH}: FD1 only; {SN,RN}, {SN,DH}: nothing. Not superkeys.
    • Every 3-subset of {CN, SN, RN, DH} contains {CN,SN} or {RN,DH}, so it gives only non-minimal superkeys.

    Both superkeys found are minimal: a proper subset either lacks SE or YR (fails by Step 1) or is one of the {SE,YR} + one-attribute sets shown above, none of which is a superkey.

    Candidate keys: K1={K_1=\{K1​={Course_no, Sec_no, Semester, Year}\}} and K2={K_2=\{K2​={Room_no, Days_hours, Semester, Year}\}}. Prime: CN, SN, SE, YR, RN, DH. Non-prime: OD, CH, CL, IS, NS.

    Step 3: normal form of RRR

    FD1: CN is a proper subset of K1K_1K1​ and OD, CH, CL are non-prime: partial dependency, so RRR is not in 2NF (1NF only). FD2 and FD3 have superkeys on the left and are fine.

    Step 4: normalize

    Split on FD1:

    • COURSE(Course_no, Offering_dept, Credit_hours, Course_level): FD1 only; key CN; BCNF.
    • SECTION(Course_no, Sec_no, Semester, Year, Days_hours, Room_no, No_of_students, Instructor_ssn): FD2, FD3 (and derived RN,DH,SE,YR→NS\text{RN,DH,SE,YR} \rightarrow \text{NS}RN,DH,SE,YR→NS); candidate keys K1K_1K1​, K2K_2K2​. Every non-trivial FD here has K1K_1K1​ or K2K_2K2​ on the left: BCNF. Course_no → COURSE.Course_no.

    Lossless: common attribute CN is the key of COURSE. Dependency-preserving: FD1 in COURSE, FD2 and FD3 in SECTION.

    Answer

    Keys of RRR: {Course_no, Sec_no, Semester, Year} and {Room_no, Days_hours, Semester, Year}. RRR is only in 1NF (FD1 is a partial dependency). Normalize to COURSE(Course_no, Offering_dept, Credit_hours, Course_level) and SECTION(Course_no, Sec_no, Semester, Year, Days_hours, Room_no, No_of_students, Instructor_ssn), with alternate key {Room_no, Days_hours, Semester, Year}; both are in BCNF, lossless and dependency-preserving.

    What the grader checks

    Both candidate keys found and justified (0.5 if only one); prime/non-prime listed; the partial dependency FD1 named as the violation; split names FD1, states the FDs in each part and the keys; BCNF check of SECTION must mention both keys (FD3 is fine because its left side is K2K_2K2​).

    14.29Natural join of ORDER and ORDER_ITEM: key, FDs, 2NF/3NFE&N Ex. 14.29 · p. 499

    Consider the following relations for an order-processing application database at ABC, Inc.

    ORDER(O#, Odate, Cust#, Total_amount)   ORDER_ITEM(O#, I#, Qty_ordered, Total_price, Discount%)

    Assume that each item has a different discount. The Total_price refers to one item, Odate is the date on which the order was placed, and the Total_amount is the amount of the order. If we apply a natural join on the relations ORDER_ITEM and ORDER in this database, what does the resulting relation schema RES look like? What will be its key? Show the FDs in this resulting relation. Is RES in 2NF? Is it in 3NF? Why or why not? (State assumptions, if you make any.)

    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. The keys are as underlined: O# for ORDER, {O#, I#} for ORDER_ITEM. Why: an order has one date, customer and amount; an item appears at most once per order.
    2. “Each item has a different discount” means the discount is set per order line, so {O#, I#}→Discount%\{\text{O\#, I\#}\} \rightarrow \text{Discount\%}{O#, I#}→Discount% but not I#→Discount%\text{I\#} \rightarrow \text{Discount\%}I#→Discount%. Why: the same item can be discounted differently on different orders. (The other reading is treated below.)
    3. Total_price is the price of that item line in that order, so it depends on {O#, I#}; no unit price is stored, and we do not assume {I#, Qty, Discount%}→Total_price\{\text{I\#, Qty, Discount\%}\} \rightarrow \text{Total\_price}{I#, Qty, Discount%}→Total_price (prices change over time).
    4. Total_amount is stored (computed as the sum of the order’s lines). That is a constraint across tuples, not an FD inside one tuple; within RES it gives only O#→Total_amount\text{O\#} \rightarrow \text{Total\_amount}O#→Total_amount.

    Schema and key

    RES(O#, I#, Odate, Cust#, Total_amount, Qty_ordered, Total_price, Discount%). Join attribute O#. Neither O# nor I# appears on a right-hand side, and {O#, I#}+\{\text{O\#, I\#}\}^+{O#, I#}+: O#→Odate, Cust#, Total_amount\text{O\#} \rightarrow \text{Odate, Cust\#, Total\_amount}O#→Odate, Cust#, Total_amount, then O#, I#→Qty_ordered, Total_price, Discount%\text{O\#, I\#} \rightarrow \text{Qty\_ordered, Total\_price, Discount\%}O#, I#→Qty_ordered, Total_price, Discount% gives everything. {O#}+={\{\text{O\#}\}^+=\{{O#}+={O#, Odate, Cust#, Total_amount}\}}, {I#}+={\{\text{I\#}\}^+=\{{I#}+={I#}\}}: neither alone is a key. Key: {O#, I#} (the only one).

    FDs in RES

    • FD1 O#→{Odate, Cust#, Total_amount}\text{O\#} \rightarrow \{\text{Odate, Cust\#, Total\_amount}\}O#→{Odate, Cust#, Total_amount} (from ORDER)
    • FD2 {O#, I#}→{Qty_ordered, Total_price, Discount%}\{\text{O\#, I\#}\} \rightarrow \{\text{Qty\_ordered, Total\_price, Discount\%}\}{O#, I#}→{Qty_ordered, Total_price, Discount%} (from ORDER_ITEM)

    2NF?

    No. FD1: O# is a proper subset of the key and Odate, Cust#, Total_amount are non-prime: partial dependency.

    3NF?

    No: 3NF requires 2NF (in the general definition, FD1 has a non-superkey left side and non-prime right side). There is no transitive dependency among the non-prime attributes under our assumptions, but the partial dependency already breaks 3NF.

    Normalizing it

    Split RES on FD1: we get back ORDER(O#, Odate, Cust#, Total_amount) and ORDER_ITEM(O#, I#, Qty_ordered, Total_price, Discount%), both BCNF; lossless since O# is the key of ORDER.

    Other reading (I#→Discount%\text{I\#} \rightarrow \text{Discount\%}I#→Discount%, a fixed discount per item): then I#→Discount%\text{I\#} \rightarrow \text{Discount\%}I#→Discount% is also a partial dependency, and the BCNF design becomes ORDER, ORDER_ITEM(O#, I#, Qty_ordered, Total_price), ITEM_DISC(I#, Discount%). The verdict on RES (1NF only) is the same.

    Answer

    RES(O#, I#, Odate, Cust#, Total_amount, Qty_ordered, Total_price, Discount%), key {O#, I#}; FDs O#→Odate, Cust#, Total_amount\text{O\#} \rightarrow \text{Odate, Cust\#, Total\_amount}O#→Odate, Cust#, Total_amount and O#, I#→Qty_ordered, Total_price, Discount%\text{O\#, I\#} \rightarrow \text{Qty\_ordered, Total\_price, Discount\%}O#, I#→Qty_ordered, Total_price, Discount%. RES is not in 2NF (O# →\to→ Odate, … is a partial dependency) and therefore not in 3NF; it is in 1NF.

    14.30CAR_SALE: normal form and successive normalizationE&N Ex. 14.30 · p. 499★ Must-do

    Consider the following relation:

    CAR_SALE(Car#, Date_sold, Salesperson#, Commission%, Discount_amt)

    Assume that a car may be sold by multiple salespeople, and hence {Car#, Salesperson#} is the primary key. Additional dependencies are

    Date_sold→Discount_amtandSalesperson#→Commission%\text{Date\_sold}\to\text{Discount\_amt}\quad\text{and}\quad\text{Salesperson\#}\to\text{Commission\%}Date_sold→Discount_amtandSalesperson#→Commission%

    Based on the given primary key, is this relation in 1NF, 2NF, or 3NF? Why or why not? How would you successively normalize it completely?

    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. Attributes are atomic, so CAR_SALE is in 1NF.
    2. The FDs are the key FD {Car#, Salesperson#}→all\{\text{Car\#, Salesperson\#}\} \rightarrow \text{all}{Car#, Salesperson#}→all, FD1 Date_sold→Discount_amt\text{Date\_sold} \rightarrow \text{Discount\_amt}Date_sold→Discount_amt, FD2 Salesperson#→Commission%\text{Salesperson\#} \rightarrow \text{Commission\%}Salesperson#→Commission%, and nothing else. Why: the question says to work “based on the given primary key”. In particular we do not assume Car#→Date_sold\text{Car\#} \rightarrow \text{Date\_sold}Car#→Date_sold (see the note at the end).

    Key check

    • {Car#, Salesperson#}+\{\text{Car\#, Salesperson\#}\}^+{Car#, Salesperson#}+ = all attributes (key FD).
    • {Car#}+={Car#}\{\text{Car\#}\}^+=\{\text{Car\#}\}{Car#}+={Car#} and {Salesperson#}+={Salesperson#, Commission%}\{\text{Salesperson\#}\}^+=\{\text{Salesperson\#, Commission\%}\}{Salesperson#}+={Salesperson#, Commission%}: neither part alone is a key, so the primary key is minimal. Both are on no right-hand side, so it is the only candidate key.
    • Prime: Car#, Salesperson#; non-prime: Date_sold, Commission%, Discount_amt.

    Normal form

    NFHolds?Reason
    1NFyesatomic attributes
    2NFnoFD2 Salesperson#→Commission%\text{Salesperson\#} \rightarrow \text{Commission\%}Salesperson#→Commission%: Salesperson# is part of the key, Commission% non-prime (partial dependency).
    3NFnonot 2NF; moreover FD1 Date_sold→Discount_amt\text{Date\_sold} \rightarrow \text{Discount\_amt}Date_sold→Discount_amt is transitive: key →\to→ Date_sold →\to→ Discount_amt, with Date_sold not a superkey and Discount_amt non-prime.

    So CAR_SALE is in 1NF only.

    Step 1: to 2NF (remove the partial dependency, FD2)

    • CS1(Car#, Salesperson#, Date_sold, Discount_amt): FDs key →\to→ Date_sold, Discount_amt and FD1. Key {Car#, Salesperson#}. 2NF (no partial dependency), not 3NF (FD1).
    • CS2(Salesperson#, Commission%): FD2; key Salesperson#. BCNF.

    Lossless: common attribute Salesperson# is the key of CS2.

    Step 2: to 3NF (remove the transitive dependency, FD1, in CS1)

    • CS1A(Car#, Salesperson#, Date_sold): FD key →\to→ Date_sold; BCNF.
    • CS1B(Date_sold, Discount_amt): FD1; key Date_sold; BCNF.

    Lossless: common attribute Date_sold is the key of CS1B.

    Answer

    CAR_SALE is in 1NF but not 2NF (Salesperson# →\to→ Commission% is partial) and not 3NF (Date_sold →\to→ Discount_amt is transitive). Final design: CS1A(Car#, Salesperson#, Date_sold), CS1B(Date_sold, Discount_amt), CS2(Salesperson#, Commission%). All are in BCNF; the decomposition is lossless and preserves FD1, FD2 and the key FD (Discount_amt is recovered via Date_sold).

    Note (alternative assumption). If a car is sold only once (on one date, possibly by several salespeople jointly), then Car#→Date_sold\text{Car\#} \rightarrow \text{Date\_sold}Car#→Date_sold also holds. It is another partial dependency, and the final design becomes (Car#, Salesperson#), (Car#, Date_sold), (Date_sold, Discount_amt), (Salesperson#, Commission%), all BCNF. State the assumption if you use it.

    What the grader checks

    Scheme as in 14.24; each NF verdict needs the violating FD and the reason (“part of key / non-prime”, “non-key →\to→ non-key”). An alternative FD (e.g. Car#→Date_sold\text{Car\#} \rightarrow \text{Date\_sold}Car#→Date_sold) earns credit only if stated as an assumption.

    14.31BOOK: normal form and normalizationE&N Ex. 14.31 · p. 499★ Must-do

    Consider the following relation for published books:

    BOOK(Book_title, Author_name, Book_type, List_price, Author_affil, Publisher)

    Author_affil refers to the affiliation of author. Suppose the following dependencies exist:

    Book_title→Publisher, Book_typeBook_type→List_priceAuthor_name→Author_affil\text{Book\_title}\to\text{Publisher, Book\_type}\quad \text{Book\_type}\to\text{List\_price}\quad \text{Author\_name}\to\text{Author\_affil}Book_title→Publisher, Book_typeBook_type→List_priceAuthor_name→Author_affil
    1. What normal form is the relation in? Explain your answer.
    2. Apply normalization until you cannot decompose the relations further. State the reasons behind each decomposition.
    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. The three FDs are complete; attributes atomic. A book may have several authors and an author several books. Why: that is why both Book_title and Author_name are needed in a tuple.
    2. Book_title identifies a book (no two books share a title). Why: implied by Book_title→Publisher\text{Book\_title} \rightarrow \text{Publisher}Book_title→Publisher.

    Closures and key

    XXXComputationX+X^+X+
    Book_title→FD1\xrightarrow{\text{FD1}}FD1​ +Publisher, Book_type →FD2\xrightarrow{\text{FD2}}FD2​ +List_price{Book_title, Publisher, Book_type, List_price}
    Author_name→FD3\xrightarrow{\text{FD3}}FD3​ +Author_affil{Author_name, Author_affil}
    Book_type→FD2\xrightarrow{\text{FD2}}FD2​ +List_price{Book_type, List_price}
    {Book_title, Author_name}FD1, FD2, FD3all six attributes

    Book_title and Author_name appear on no right-hand side, so they are in every key; together they are a superkey, and neither alone is (closures above). Key: {Book_title, Author_name} (the only one). Prime: Book_title, Author_name. Non-prime: Book_type, List_price, Author_affil, Publisher.

    (a) Normal form

    1NF: atomic. 2NF fails: FD1 Book_title→Publisher, Book_type\text{Book\_title} \rightarrow \text{Publisher, Book\_type}Book_title→Publisher, Book_type and FD3 Author_name→Author_affil\text{Author\_name} \rightarrow \text{Author\_affil}Author_name→Author_affil have a proper part of the key on the left and non-prime attributes on the right (partial dependencies). Hence BOOK is in 1NF only. (FD2 is also a transitive dependency, a 3NF violation.)

    (b) Normalization

    1. 2NF, split on FD3 (partial dependency on Author_name): AUTHOR(Author_name, Author_affil) with FD3; the rest (Book_title, Author_name, Book_type, List_price, Publisher). Common attribute Author_name = key of AUTHOR.
    2. 2NF, split on Book_title→Publisher, Book_type, List_price\text{Book\_title} \rightarrow \text{Publisher, Book\_type, List\_price}Book_title→Publisher, Book_type, List_price (partial dependency, using the closure of Book_title): BOOK_INFO(Book_title, Publisher, Book_type, List_price) with FD1, FD2; and BOOK_AUTHOR(Book_title, Author_name) with no non-trivial FD. Common attribute Book_title = key of BOOK_INFO.
      Now all relations are in 2NF. BOOK_INFO is not in 3NF: FD2 Book_type→List_price\text{Book\_type} \rightarrow \text{List\_price}Book_type→List_price, Book_type is not a superkey, List_price non-prime (transitive Book_title →\to→ Book_type →\to→ List_price).
    3. 3NF, split BOOK_INFO on FD2: BOOK_TYPE(Book_type, List_price) with FD2, and BOOK1(Book_title, Publisher, Book_type) with FD1. Common attribute Book_type = key of BOOK_TYPE.

    Each final relation has only FDs whose left side is its key (BOOK_AUTHOR has none), so all are in BCNF and cannot usefully be decomposed further.

    Answer

    (a) 1NF (partial dependencies FD1, FD3 on the key {Book_title, Author_name}). (b) BOOK_AUTHOR(Book_title, Author_name), BOOK1(Book_title, Publisher, Book_type), BOOK_TYPE(Book_type, List_price), AUTHOR(Author_name, Author_affil); all BCNF, lossless (each split on a key of one side), dependency-preserving (FD1 in BOOK1, FD2 in BOOK_TYPE, FD3 in AUTHOR).

    Watch out

    Leaving out BOOK_AUTHOR(Book_title, Author_name). Then nothing records who wrote which book: the decomposition is lossy (rubric: 0 if lossy).

    What the grader checks

    Scheme as in 14.24; 0 for the final mark if any final relation is not in 3NF (e.g. keeping List_price with Book_title).

    14.32Business statements to FDs: DISK_DRIVEE&N Ex. 14.32 · p. 500

    This exercise asks you to convert business statements into dependencies. Consider the relation DISK_DRIVE(Serial_number, Manufacturer, Model, Batch, Capacity, Retailer). Each tuple in the relation DISK_DRIVE contains information about a disk drive with a unique Serial_number, made by a manufacturer, with a particular model number, released in a certain batch, which has a certain storage capacity and is sold by a certain retailer. For example, the tuple Disk_drive (‘1978619’, ‘WesternDigital’, ‘A2235X’, ‘765234’, 500, ‘CompUSA’) specifies that WesternDigital made a disk drive with serial number 1978619 and model number A2235X, released in batch 765234; it is 500GB and sold by CompUSA. Write each of the following dependencies as an FD:

    1. The manufacturer and serial number uniquely identifies the drive.
    2. A model number is registered by a manufacturer and therefore can’t be used by another manufacturer.
    3. All disk drives in a particular batch are the same model.
    4. All disk drives of a certain model of a particular manufacturer have exactly the same capacity.
    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. “Uniquely identifies the drive” means it determines every other attribute of the tuple.
    2. Batch numbers are globally unique (not reused across manufacturers). Why: statement (c) speaks of “a particular batch” without qualifying it by manufacturer.
    1. {Manufacturer, Serial_number}→{Model, Batch, Capacity, Retailer}\{\text{Manufacturer, Serial\_number}\} \rightarrow \{\text{Model, Batch, Capacity, Retailer}\}{Manufacturer, Serial_number}→{Model, Batch, Capacity, Retailer}
    2. Model→Manufacturer\text{Model} \rightarrow \text{Manufacturer}Model→Manufacturer
    3. Batch→Model\text{Batch} \rightarrow \text{Model}Batch→Model
    4. {Model, Manufacturer}→Capacity\{\text{Model, Manufacturer}\} \rightarrow \text{Capacity}{Model, Manufacturer}→Capacity

    Remarks. With (b), Manufacturer is extraneous in (d): {Model}+\{\text{Model}\}^+{Model}+ = {Model, Manufacturer, Capacity} (b then d), so (d) is equivalent to Model→Capacity\text{Model} \rightarrow \text{Capacity}Model→Capacity. Also {Batch}+\{\text{Batch}\}^+{Batch}+ = {Batch, Model, Manufacturer, Capacity}. Candidate keys (computed): {Serial_number, Manufacturer}, {Serial_number, Model}, {Serial_number, Batch}. If, as the description says, Serial_number alone is unique, then Serial_number→all\text{Serial\_number} \rightarrow \text{all}Serial_number→all and Serial_number is the only key.

    Answer

    (a) Manufacturer, Serial_number →\to→ Model, Batch, Capacity, Retailer; (b) Model →\to→ Manufacturer; (c) Batch →\to→ Model; (d) Model, Manufacturer →\to→ Capacity (equivalently Model →\to→ Capacity, given (b)).

    Watch out

    Writing (b) as Manufacturer→Model\text{Manufacturer} \rightarrow \text{Model}Manufacturer→Model: a manufacturer has many models. “A model can’t be used by another manufacturer” means each model has one manufacturer.

    14.33Doctor visits: 2NF, then 3NFE&N Ex. 14.33 · p. 500★ Must-do

    Consider the following relation:

    R(Doctor#, Patient#, Date, Diagnosis, Treat_code, Charge)

    In the above relation, a tuple describes a visit of a patient to a doctor along with a treatment code and daily charge. Assume that diagnosis is determined (uniquely) for each patient by a doctor. Assume that each treatment code has a fixed charge (regardless of patient). Is this relation in 2NF? Justify your answer and decompose if necessary. Then argue whether further normalization to 3NF is necessary, and if so, perform it.

    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. A patient visits a given doctor at most once per date, and each visit has one treatment code. Why: a tuple is “a visit”; so {Doctor#, Patient#, Date} identifies a tuple.
    2. “Diagnosis is determined for each patient by a doctor” gives {Doctor#, Patient#}→Diagnosis\{\text{Doctor\#, Patient\#}\} \rightarrow \text{Diagnosis}{Doctor#, Patient#}→Diagnosis (the same over all visits of that pair).
    3. “Each treatment code has a fixed charge” gives Treat_code→Charge\text{Treat\_code} \rightarrow \text{Charge}Treat_code→Charge.
    4. No other FDs (e.g. the diagnosis does not fix the treatment).

    FDs: FD1 {Doctor#, Patient#, Date}→{Treat_code, Charge, Diagnosis}\{\text{Doctor\#, Patient\#, Date}\} \rightarrow \{\text{Treat\_code, Charge, Diagnosis}\}{Doctor#, Patient#, Date}→{Treat_code, Charge, Diagnosis}; FD2 {Doctor#, Patient#}→Diagnosis\{\text{Doctor\#, Patient\#}\} \rightarrow \text{Diagnosis}{Doctor#, Patient#}→Diagnosis; FD3 Treat_code→Charge\text{Treat\_code} \rightarrow \text{Charge}Treat_code→Charge.

    Key

    Doctor#, Patient#, Date are on no right-hand side, so they are in every key. Their closure: →FD1\xrightarrow{\text{FD1}}FD1​ +Treat_code, Charge, Diagnosis =R=R=R. So {Doctor#, Patient#, Date} is the only candidate key. Prime: Doctor#, Patient#, Date; non-prime: Diagnosis, Treat_code, Charge.

    2NF?

    No. FD2: {Doctor#, Patient#} is a proper subset of the key and Diagnosis is non-prime: partial dependency. ({Doctor#, Patient#}+^++ = {Doctor#, Patient#, Diagnosis}, so nothing else is partially dependent.) Split on FD2:

    • R1(Doctor#, Patient#, Diagnosis): FD2; key {Doctor#, Patient#}; BCNF.
    • R2(Doctor#, Patient#, Date, Treat_code, Charge): FD1 restricted (key →\to→ Treat_code, Charge) and FD3; key {Doctor#, Patient#, Date}. In 2NF: no part of the key determines Treat_code or Charge.

    Lossless: common attributes {Doctor#, Patient#} are the key of R1.

    3NF needed?

    Yes. In R2, FD3 Treat_code→Charge\text{Treat\_code} \rightarrow \text{Charge}Treat_code→Charge: Treat_code is not a superkey of R2 and Charge is non-prime: transitive dependency key →\to→ Treat_code →\to→ Charge (a treatment’s charge is repeated in every visit; changing it means updating many tuples). Split R2 on FD3:

    • R2A(Doctor#, Patient#, Date, Treat_code): key →\to→ Treat_code; BCNF.
    • R2B(Treat_code, Charge): FD3; BCNF.

    Lossless: Treat_code is the key of R2B.

    Answer

    Not in 2NF (Doctor#, Patient# →\to→ Diagnosis is partial). 2NF: R1(Doctor#, Patient#, Diagnosis), R2(Doctor#, Patient#, Date, Treat_code, Charge). R2 is not in 3NF (Treat_code →\to→ Charge is transitive), so 3NF is needed: R1, R2A(Doctor#, Patient#, Date, Treat_code), R2B(Treat_code, Charge). All BCNF, lossless, dependency-preserving.

    What the grader checks

    FDs derived from the English with each assumption stated; key justified; 2NF verdict with the violating FD and reason (part of key, non-prime); split with FDs and keys of each part; explicit argument that R2 still violates 3NF (Treat_code →\to→ Charge) and the second split; lossless justified at each split.

    14.34CAR_SALE options: not 3NF, not even 2NFE&N Ex. 14.34 · p. 500

    Consider the following relation:

    CAR_SALE(Car_id, Option_type, Option_listprice, Sale_date, Option_discountedprice)

    This relation refers to options installed in cars (e.g., cruise control) that were sold at a dealership, and the list and discounted prices of the options. If CarID →\to→ Sale_date and Option_type →\to→ Option_listprice and CarID, Option_type →\to→ Option_discountedprice, argue using the generalized definition of the 3NF that this relation is not in 3NF. Then argue from your knowledge of 2NF, why it is not even in 2NF.

    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. “CarID” in the FDs is the attribute Car_id. The three FDs are complete.

    FDs: FD1 Car_id→Sale_date\text{Car\_id} \rightarrow \text{Sale\_date}Car_id→Sale_date; FD2 Option_type→Option_listprice\text{Option\_type} \rightarrow \text{Option\_listprice}Option_type→Option_listprice; FD3 {Car_id, Option_type}→Option_discountedprice\{\text{Car\_id, Option\_type}\} \rightarrow \text{Option\_discountedprice}{Car_id, Option_type}→Option_discountedprice.

    Key

    Car_id and Option_type are on no right-hand side, so both are in every key. {Car_id, Option_type}+\{\text{Car\_id, Option\_type}\}^+{Car_id, Option_type}+: FD1 +Sale_date, FD2 +Option_listprice, FD3 +Option_discountedprice =R=R=R. {Car_id}+\{\text{Car\_id}\}^{+}{Car_id}+ = {Car_id, Sale_date}, {Option_type}+\{\text{Option\_type}\}^{+}{Option_type}+ = {Option_type, Option_listprice}. Key {Car_id, Option_type} (only one). Prime: Car_id, Option_type; non-prime: Sale_date, Option_listprice, Option_discountedprice.

    Not in 3NF (general definition)

    3NF requires, for every non-trivial X→AX \rightarrow AX→A: XXX is a superkey or AAA is prime.

    • FD1: Car_id is not a superkey (its closure lacks Option_type, …) and Sale_date is non-prime: violates 3NF.
    • FD2: Option_type is not a superkey and Option_listprice is non-prime: violates 3NF.

    (FD3 is fine: its left side is the key.)

    Not even in 2NF

    2NF requires every non-prime attribute to be fully dependent on every key. Sale_date depends on Car_id, a proper subset of the key (FD1), and Option_listprice on Option_type, another proper subset (FD2). These are partial dependencies, so 2NF fails. (Exactly the 3NF violations above whose left side is part of a key are 2NF violations.)

    Remedy

    Split on FD1 and FD2: CAR(Car_id, Sale_date), OPTION(Option_type, Option_listprice), CAR_OPTION(Car_id, Option_type, Option_discountedprice). All BCNF; lossless (each split on a key of one side); every FD preserved.

    Answer

    Key {Car_id, Option_type}. Car_id →\to→ Sale_date and Option_type →\to→ Option_listprice have non-superkey left sides and non-prime right sides, so 3NF fails. Since each left side is a proper part of the key, they are partial dependencies, so 2NF fails as well: CAR_SALE is in 1NF only.

    What the grader checks

    Key found with closures; for 3NF, quote the definition and show both conditions fail (not a superkey and non-prime); for 2NF, name the partial dependency (proper subset of key →\to→ non-prime).

    9  Chapter 15 exercises

    Textbook exercises

    How this section is organised

    15.1–15.12 are review questions: each answer gives the definition, the key point a grader looks for, and a small worked example. Between them they also give one worked run of every Chapter 15 algorithm: attribute closure (Alg. 15.1) and finding a key (Alg. 15.2(a)) are in 15.3; minimal cover (Alg. 15.2) is in 15.5; the chase (Alg. 15.3) is in 15.10; 3NF synthesis (Alg. 15.4) and BCNF decomposition (Alg. 15.5) are in 15.11. 15.21 and 15.24 (past-paper material, with 15.5 and 15.10) are computational and fully worked.

    15.1Role of Armstrong’s inference rulesE&N Ex. 15.1 · p. 534

    What is the role of Armstrong’s inference rules (inference rules IR1 through IR3) in the development of the theory of relational design?

    Solution · written for this guide

    The rules. For attribute sets X,Y,Z,WX,Y,Z,WX,Y,Z,W of RRR:

    RuleStatementName
    IR1if X⊇YX \supseteq YX⊇Y then X→YX\to YX→Yreflexive (gives the trivial FDs)
    IR2{X→Y}⊨XZ→YZ\{X\to Y\}\models XZ\to YZ{X→Y}⊨XZ→YZaugmentation
    IR3{X→Y, Y→Z}⊨X→Z\{X\to Y,\ Y\to Z\}\models X\to Z{X→Y, Y→Z}⊨X→Ztransitive
    IR4{X→YZ}⊨X→Y\{X\to YZ\}\models X\to Y{X→YZ}⊨X→Ydecomposition (projective)
    IR5{X→Y, X→Z}⊨X→YZ\{X\to Y,\ X\to Z\}\models X\to YZ{X→Y, X→Z}⊨X→YZunion (additive)
    IR6{X→Y, WY→Z}⊨WX→Z\{X\to Y,\ WY\to Z\}\models WX\to Z{X→Y, WY→Z}⊨WX→Zpseudotransitive

    Their role. A designer writes down only the FDs that are semantically obvious (a set FFF), but many more FDs hold in every legal state (the closure F+F^+F+). Armstrong’s rules are the mechanism for deriving F+F^+F+ from FFF, and because they are sound and complete (15.2) they derive exactly F+F^+F+. The rest of design theory builds on this:

    • Attribute closure X+X^+X+ (Alg. 15.1) is a systematic application of IR1, IR3 and IR4; the fact “X→Y∈F+  ⟺  Y⊆X+X\to Y\in F^+ \iff Y\subseteq X^+X→Y∈F+⟺Y⊆X+” is what makes F+F^+F+ computable without listing it.
    • Keys: XXX is a superkey iff X→RX\to RX→R is derivable, i.e. X+=RX^+=RX+=R (Alg. 15.2(a)).
    • Equivalence and covers (15.4): E≡FE\equiv FE≡F iff each derives every FD of the other.
    • Minimal cover (Alg. 15.2): IR4 splits right-hand sides; extraneous attributes and redundant FDs are those whose removal leaves F+F^+F+ unchanged.
    • Normal-form tests (2NF/3NF/BCNF are defined over all FDs in F+F^+F+, not just those listed), projection of FDs onto a relation, dependency preservation and the lossless-join tests (NJB: is (R1∩R2)→(R1−R2)(R_1\cap R_2)\to(R_1-R_2)(R1​∩R2​)→(R1​−R2​) in F+F^+F+?) all need F+F^+F+.
    • The design algorithms 15.4 (3NF synthesis) and 15.5 (BCNF decomposition) take FFF as input and rely on all of the above.

    Proofs of IR4–IR6 from IR1–IR3

    IR4: X→YZ⊨X→YX\to YZ \models X\to YX→YZ⊨X→YIR5: X→Y, X→Z⊨X→YZX\to Y,\,X\to Z\models X\to YZX→Y,X→Z⊨X→YZIR6: X→Y, WY→Z⊨WX→ZX\to Y,\,WY\to Z\models WX\to ZX→Y,WY→Z⊨WX→Z
    1. X→YZX\to YZX→YZ (given)
    2. YZ→YYZ\to YYZ→Y (IR1, YZ⊇YYZ\supseteq YYZ⊇Y)
    3. X→YX\to YX→Y (IR3 on 1, 2)    		1. X→YX\to YX→Y, 2. X→ZX\to ZX→Z (given)
    3. X→XYX\to XYX→XY (IR2 on 1 with XXX; XX=XXX=XXX=X)
    4. XY→YZXY\to YZXY→YZ (IR2 on 2 with YYY)
    5. X→YZX\to YZX→YZ (IR3 on 3, 4)    		1. X→YX\to YX→Y, 2. WY→ZWY\to ZWY→Z (given)
    3. WX→WYWX\to WYWX→WY (IR2 on 1 with WWW)
    4. WX→ZWX\to ZWX→Z (IR3 on 3, 2)
    Rules that do not exist

    X→AX\to AX→A and Y→BY\to BY→B give XY→ABXY\to ABXY→AB (augment and union), but XY→AXY\to AXY→A does not give X→AX\to AX→A or Y→AY\to AY→A (there is no “left-side decomposition”). And FDs are not symmetric: X→YX\to YX→Y does not give Y→XY\to XY→X.

    Answer

    IR1–IR3 are the (sound and complete) rules for inferring every FD implied by a given set FFF, i.e. for computing F+F^+F+. Closure of attribute sets, keys, equivalence, minimal covers, the normal-form tests, dependency preservation, the lossless-join tests and the synthesis/decomposition algorithms are all defined in terms of F+F^+F+ and so all rest on these rules. IR4–IR6 are derived rules (proved above).

    15.2Soundness and completenessE&N Ex. 15.2 · p. 534

    What is meant by the completeness and soundness of Armstrong’s inference rules?

    Solution · written for this guide

    Write F⊢X→YF\vdash X\to YF⊢X→Y for “X→YX\to YX→Y can be derived from FFF by IR1–IR3” and F⊨X→YF\models X\to YF⊨X→Y for “X→YX\to YX→Y holds in every relation state that satisfies FFF”.

    • Sound: F⊢X→Y⇒F⊨X→YF\vdash X\to Y \Rightarrow F\models X\to YF⊢X→Y⇒F⊨X→Y. Every derived FD really holds in every legal state: the rules never produce a false dependency.
    • Complete: F⊨X→Y⇒F⊢X→YF\models X\to Y \Rightarrow F\vdash X\to YF⊨X→Y⇒F⊢X→Y. Every FD that is implied by FFF can be derived: repeating IR1–IR3 until nothing new appears yields all of F+F^+F+, nothing is missed.

    Together: derivable = implied, so F+F^+F+ can be computed purely syntactically.

    Why sound (each rule preserves truth in any state rrr)

    IR1: if t1[X]=t2[X]t_1[X]=t_2[X]t1​[X]=t2​[X] and Y⊆XY\subseteq XY⊆X then t1[Y]=t2[Y]t_1[Y]=t_2[Y]t1​[Y]=t2​[Y]. IR2 (by contradiction): suppose X→YX\to YX→Y holds but t1[XZ]=t2[XZ]t_1[XZ]=t_2[XZ]t1​[XZ]=t2​[XZ], t1[YZ]≠t2[YZ]t_1[YZ]\ne t_2[YZ]t1​[YZ]=t2​[YZ]. From t1[X]=t2[X]t_1[X]=t_2[X]t1​[X]=t2​[X] we get t1[Y]=t2[Y]t_1[Y]=t_2[Y]t1​[Y]=t2​[Y], and t1[Z]=t2[Z]t_1[Z]=t_2[Z]t1​[Z]=t2​[Z], so t1[YZ]=t2[YZ]t_1[YZ]=t_2[YZ]t1​[YZ]=t2​[YZ]: contradiction. IR3: t1[X]=t2[X]⇒t1[Y]=t2[Y]⇒t1[Z]=t2[Z]t_1[X]=t_2[X]\Rightarrow t_1[Y]=t_2[Y]\Rightarrow t_1[Z]=t_2[Z]t1​[X]=t2​[X]⇒t1​[Y]=t2​[Y]⇒t1​[Z]=t2​[Z]. A derivation is a finite chain of such steps, so every derived FD holds.

    Why complete (sketch)

    Suppose X→YX\to YX→Y cannot be derived. Let X+X^+X+ be the closure of XXX under FFF (Alg. 15.1; every attribute it adds is derivable, so X→X+X\to X^+X→X+ is derivable and Y⊈X+Y\not\subseteq X^+Y⊆X+). Build a state with two tuples that agree exactly on X+X^+X+ and differ on every other attribute. For any V→WV\to WV→W in FFF: if V⊈X+V\not\subseteq X^+V⊆X+ the tuples disagree on VVV and the FD holds vacuously; if V⊆X+V\subseteq X^+V⊆X+ then the closure algorithm puts WWW in X+X^+X+, so the tuples agree on WWW and the FD holds. So the state satisfies FFF but violates X→YX\to YX→Y (the tuples agree on XXX, differ on Y−X+≠∅Y-X^+\ne\emptysetY−X+=∅). Hence X→YX\to YX→Y is not implied either. Contrapositive: implied ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ derivable.

    Answer

    Sound: anything derived with IR1–IR3 from FFF holds in every relation state satisfying FFF. Complete: every FD that holds in all such states (all of F+F^+F+) can be derived with IR1–IR3. So F+F^+F+ is exactly the set of FDs derivable by Armstrong’s rules.

    15.3Closure of a set of FDsE&N Ex. 15.3 · p. 534

    What is meant by the closure of a set of functional dependencies? Illustrate with an example.

    Solution · written for this guide
    Definition: Closure F+F^+F+ and attribute closure X+X^+X+

    F+F^+F+ is the set of all FDs implied by FFF: FFF itself plus every FD that can be inferred from it (equivalently, by 15.2, derived with IR1–IR3). It includes trivial FDs such as X→XX\to XX→X. For an attribute set XXX, X+X^+X+ is the set of all attributes functionally determined by XXX under FFF. They are linked by:   X→Y∈F+  ⟺  Y⊆X+\;X\to Y\in F^+ \iff Y\subseteq X^+X→Y∈F+⟺Y⊆X+.

    F+F^+F+ is huge (exponential in the number of attributes), so we never list it; we compute X+X^+X+ for the XXX we care about with Algorithm 15.1: start with X+:=XX^+:=XX+:=X; repeatedly, for each Y→ZY\to ZY→Z in FFF with Y⊆X+Y\subseteq X^+Y⊆X+, add ZZZ; stop when a full pass adds nothing.

    Example

    R(A,B,C,D,E)R(A,B,C,D,E)R(A,B,C,D,E), F={A→B, B→C, CD→E}F=\{A \rightarrow B,\ B \rightarrow C,\ CD \rightarrow E\}F={A→B, B→C, CD→E}.

    XXXComputation (Alg. 15.1)X+X^+X+
    AAAstart AAA; A→BA\to BA→B adds BBB; B→CB\to CB→C adds CCC; CD→ECD\to ECD→E needs DDDABCABCABC
    BBBB→CB\to CB→C adds CCCBCBCBC
    CDCDCDCD→ECD\to ECD→E adds EEECDECDECDE
    DDDno FD appliesDDD
    ADADADA→BA\to BA→B: ABDABDABD; B→CB\to CB→C: ABCDABCDABCD; CD→ECD\to ECD→E: ABCDEABCDEABCDEABCDE=RABCDE=RABCDE=R

    Some members of F+F^+F+ that are not in FFF: A→CA\to CA→C (IR3), A→ABCA\to ABCA→ABC (from A+A^+A+), AD→EAD\to EAD→E (IR6 using A→CA\to CA→C and CD→ECD\to ECD→E), BD→EBD\to EBD→E, AD→ABCDEAD\to ABCDEAD→ABCDE, and trivial ones like AB→AAB\to AAB→A. Counting every X→YX\to YX→Y with X,YX,YX,Y non-empty and Y⊆X+Y\subseteq X^+Y⊆X+, this 3-FD set has ∣F+∣=439|F^+|=439∣F+∣=439 (checked by program), which is why we work with X+X^+X+ instead.

    Using closures to find a key (Algorithm 15.2(a))

    Start with K=ABCDEK=ABCDEK=ABCDE and try to drop each attribute in order, keeping the drop if (K−{x})+=R(K-\{x\})^+=R(K−{x})+=R: drop AAA: (BCDE)+=BCDE(BCDE)^+=BCDE(BCDE)+=BCDE, no; drop BBB: (ACDE)+=R(ACDE)^+=R(ACDE)+=R, yes, K=ACDEK=ACDEK=ACDE; drop CCC: (ADE)+=R(ADE)^+=R(ADE)+=R, yes, K=ADEK=ADEK=ADE; drop DDD: (AE)+=ABCE(AE)^+=ABCE(AE)+=ABCE, no; drop EEE: (AD)+=R(AD)^+=R(AD)+=R, yes. Key K=ADK=ADK=AD. (Here it is the only key: AAA and DDD are on no right-hand side, so they are in every key, and ADADAD is already a key.)

    Answer

    F+F^+F+ = all FDs implied by FFF (all derivable with IR1–IR3). It is described compactly by attribute closures: X→Y∈F+X\to Y\in F^+X→Y∈F+ iff Y⊆X+Y\subseteq X^+Y⊆X+. Example above: A+=ABCA^+=ABCA+=ABC, (AD)+=R(AD)^+=R(AD)+=R, so A→CA\to CA→C and AD→EAD\to EAD→E are in F+F^+F+ and ADADAD is the key.

    15.4Equivalence of FD setsE&N Ex. 15.4 · p. 534

    When are two sets of functional dependencies equivalent? How can we determine their equivalence?

    Solution · written for this guide
    Definition: Cover and equivalence

    FFF covers EEE if every FD in EEE is in F+F^+F+. EEE and FFF are equivalent if E+=F+E^+=F^+E+=F+, i.e. FFF covers EEE and EEE covers FFF.

    Test (no need to build E+E^+E+ or F+F^+F+): for each X→YX\to YX→Y in EEE compute X+X^+X+ under FFF and check Y⊆X+Y\subseteq X^+Y⊆X+; then do the same the other way round. Equivalent iff all checks pass.

    Example (the book’s: show F≡GF\equiv GF≡G)

    F={A→C, AC→D, E→AD, E→H}F=\{A \rightarrow C,\ AC \rightarrow D,\ E \rightarrow AD,\ E \rightarrow H\}F={A→C, AC→D, E→AD, E→H},   G={A→CD, E→AH}G=\{A \rightarrow CD,\ E \rightarrow AH\}G={A→CD, E→AH}.

    Does GGG cover FFF?closure under GGGOK?
    A→CA\to CA→CAG+=ACDA^+_G=ACDAG+​=ACDC∈C\inC∈yes
    AC→DAC\to DAC→D(AC)G+=ACD(AC)^+_G=ACD(AC)G+​=ACDD∈D\inD∈yes
    E→ADE\to ADE→ADEG+E^+_GEG+​: E→AHE\to AHE→AH gives AEHAEHAEH, A→CDA\to CDA→CD gives ACDEHACDEHACDEHAD⊆AD\subseteqAD⊆yes
    E→HE\to HE→HEG+=ACDEHE^+_G=ACDEHEG+​=ACDEHH∈H\inH∈yes
    Does FFF cover GGG?closure under FFF
    A→CDA\to CDA→CDAF+A^+_FAF+​: A→CA\to CA→C gives ACACAC, AC→DAC\to DAC→D gives ACDACDACDCD⊆CD\subseteqCD⊆yes
    E→AHE\to AHE→AHEF+E^+_FEF+​: E→ADE\to ADE→AD, E→HE\to HE→H give ADEHADEHADEH; A→CA\to CA→C gives ACDEHACDEHACDEHAH⊆AH\subseteqAH⊆yes
    Answer

    EEE and FFF are equivalent when E+=F+E^+=F^+E+=F+, i.e. each covers the other. Test it by computing, for every FD X→YX\to YX→Y of one set, X+X^+X+ under the other set and checking Y⊆X+Y\subseteq X^+Y⊆X+. In the example both directions pass, so F≡GF\equiv GF≡G.

    Watch out

    Checking only one direction proves only “covers”, not equivalence. And the closure must be computed under the other set, not the set the FD came from.

    15.5Minimal sets of FDsE&N Ex. 15.5 · p. 534★ Must-do

    What is a minimal set of functional dependencies? Does every set of dependencies have a minimal equivalent set? Is it always unique?

    Solution · written for this guide
    Definition: Minimal set of FDs; minimal cover

    FFF is minimal if (1) every FD in FFF has a single attribute on its right-hand side; (2) no FD X→AX\to AX→A can be replaced by Y→AY\to AY→A with Y⊊XY\subsetneq XY⊊X and still give a set equivalent to FFF (no extraneous left-hand attribute); (3) no FD can be removed and still give a set equivalent to FFF (no redundant FD). A minimal cover of EEE is a minimal set FFF with F≡EF\equiv EF≡E.

    Does one always exist? Yes. Algorithm 15.2 constructs one for any finite EEE: each step replaces the set by an equivalent one and only ever shrinks it (fewer attributes or fewer FDs), so it terminates, and at the end no step applies, which is exactly conditions (1)–(3).

    Is it unique? No. The result depends on the order in which FDs and attributes are tested. Example: E={A→BC, B→AC, C→AB}E=\{A \rightarrow BC,\ B \rightarrow AC,\ C \rightarrow AB\}E={A→BC, B→AC, C→AB} (AAA, BBB, CCC all determine each other). All of

    {A→B, B→C, C→A},{A→C, C→B, B→A},{A→C, B→C, C→A, C→B}\{A\to B,\ B\to C,\ C\to A\},\quad \{A\to C,\ C\to B,\ B\to A\},\quad \{A\to C,\ B\to C,\ C\to A,\ C\to B\}{A→B, B→C, C→A},{A→C, C→B, B→A},{A→C, B→C, C→A, C→B}

    are minimal covers of EEE (each equivalent to EEE and minimal; checked by program). The third, with 4 FDs, is what Alg. 15.2 gives if it tests in the order A→B,A→C,B→A,…A\to B, A\to C, B\to A,\dotsA→B,A→C,B→A,…; it is still minimal (no single FD can be removed) even though a 3-FD cover exists. “Minimal” means non-redundant, not minimum-size; the book suggests preferring the cover with the fewest FDs if a choice is needed.

    Worked run of Algorithm 15.2

    E={A→BC, B→C, AB→D}E=\{A \rightarrow BC,\ B \rightarrow C,\ AB \rightarrow D\}E={A→BC, B→C, AB→D}.

    1. Split right sides (IR4): A→B, A→C, B→C, AB→DA\to B,\ A\to C,\ B\to C,\ AB\to DA→B, A→C, B→C, AB→D.
    2. Extraneous left-hand attributes (only AB→DAB\to DAB→D has two). Is BBB extraneous? A+=ABCDA^+=ABCDA+=ABCD (via A→BA\to BA→B, A→CA\to CA→C, AB→DAB\to DAB→D) contains DDD: yes, replace by A→DA\to DA→D. (Is AAA extraneous? B+=BCB^+=BCB+=BC lacks DDD: no; but BBB was already removed.) Set now: A→B, A→C, B→C, A→DA\to B,\ A\to C,\ B\to C,\ A\to DA→B, A→C, B→C, A→D.

    3. Redundant FDs: for each FD, compute the closure of its left side under the current set without it.

      FD testedLHS closure without itRHS reached?Decision
      A→BA\to BA→BA+=ACDA^+=ACDA+=ACDnokeep
      A→CA\to CA→CA+A^+A+: A→BA\to BA→B, B→CB\to CB→C, A→DA\to DA→D: ABCDABCDABCDyesremove
      B→CB\to CB→CB+=BB^+=BB+=Bnokeep
      A→DA\to DA→DA+=ABCA^+=ABCA+=ABCnokeep

    Minimal cover {A→B, B→C, A→D}\{A\to B,\ B\to C,\ A\to D\}{A→B, B→C, A→D} (grouped: {A→BD, B→C}\{A\to BD,\ B\to C\}{A→BD, B→C}). Check: under it A+=ABCDA^+=ABCDA+=ABCD, B+=BCB^+=BCB+=BC, which recovers every FD of EEE; so it is equivalent.

    Order of the steps matters

    Do the left-side (extraneous attribute) step before the redundancy step. With {A→C, AC→D, D→C}\{A\to C,\ AC\to D,\ D\to C\}{A→C, AC→D, D→C}, testing redundancy first removes nothing; then reducing AC→DAC\to DAC→D to A→DA\to DA→D leaves {A→C, A→D, D→C}\{A\to C,\ A\to D,\ D\to C\}{A→C, A→D, D→C}, in which A→CA\to CA→C is now redundant: not minimal. The correct order gives {A→D, D→C}\{A\to D,\ D\to C\}{A→D, D→C}. Also, test each FD against the current, already reduced set: two FDs may each be redundant on their own but not both together.

    Answer

    A minimal set has single-attribute right sides, no extraneous left-side attributes and no redundant FDs. Every set EEE has at least one minimal equivalent set (Algorithm 15.2 always finds one), but it is not unique in general: different testing orders can give different (even different-sized) minimal covers.

    What the grader checks (N-I rubric Q2(c), GA4 3(c))

    Split RHS (1): rewrite as single-attribute right sides; 0 if skipped. LHS checked (1): for each multi-attribute left side, show the closure test for each attribute; if all left sides are single attributes, say so (0 if not mentioned). Redundancy tests (2): a closure test for every FD against the current set; 1 if some tests are missing; 0 if an essential FD is removed. Final cover (1): must be equivalent and minimal. Covers are not unique: graders verify, they do not match, so any correct cover with working gets full marks.

    15.6Attribute preservationE&N Ex. 15.6 · p. 534

    What is meant by the attribute preservation condition on a decomposition?

    Solution · written for this guide

    A decomposition of the universal relation RRR is a set of schemas D={R1,…,Rm}D=\{R_1,\dots,R_m\}D={R1​,…,Rm​} with each Ri⊆RR_i\subseteq RRi​⊆R. Attribute preservation requires

    R1∪R2∪⋯∪Rm  =  R,R_1\cup R_2\cup\dots\cup R_m \;=\; R,R1​∪R2​∪⋯∪Rm​=R,

    i.e. every attribute of RRR appears in at least one RiR_iRi​, so no attribute (and no information about it) is lost by the decomposition. (Attributes may appear in several RiR_iRi​; the shared ones are the join attributes.)

    Example: EMP_PROJ(Ssn, Pnumber, Hours, Ename, Pname, Plocation) decomposed into EMP(Ssn, Ename), PROJ(Pnumber, Pname, Plocation), WORKS_ON(Ssn, Pnumber, Hours) preserves attributes; dropping WORKS_ON would lose Hours.

    Answer

    The union of the attributes of the decomposed schemas must equal the attributes of the original schema: no attribute may be dropped. It is the most basic requirement; it says nothing about spurious tuples or lost dependencies (see 15.8, 15.10).

    15.7Why normal forms alone are not enoughE&N Ex. 15.7 · p. 534

    Why are normal forms alone insufficient as a condition for a good schema design?

    Solution · written for this guide

    A normal form is a property of each relation on its own. A good design is a property of the decomposition as a whole: the relations together must still represent exactly the original data and its constraints. Normal forms say nothing about this.

    • Spurious tuples. EMP_LOCS(Ename, Plocation) is in BCNF (every 2-attribute schema is), and EMP_PROJ1(Ssn, Pnumber, Hours, Pname, Plocation) is a valid relation, yet joining them on Plocation produces spurious tuples (Fig. 14.6): the decomposition is lossy. At the extreme, splitting any RRR into one-attribute relations puts every relation in BCNF, but the join is a Cartesian product and all associations are lost.
    • Lost constraints. LOTS1A split into LOTS1AX(Property_id, Area, Lot#) and LOTS1AY(Area, County) is all-BCNF, but FD2 {County, Lot#} →\to→ Property_id can no longer be checked inside one relation.

    So, in addition to each RiR_iRi​ being in 3NF/BCNF, the decomposition must satisfy attribute preservation (15.6), the nonadditive (lossless) join property (15.10, essential) and, preferably, dependency preservation (15.8).

    Answer

    Normal forms test relations individually; they cannot detect that a set of relations is lossy (spurious tuples on join) or has lost FDs. A good design also needs the decomposition-level properties: attribute preservation, nonadditive join (mandatory) and dependency preservation (desirable).

    15.8Dependency preservationE&N Ex. 15.8 · p. 534

    What is the dependency preservation property for a decomposition? Why is it important?

    Solution · written for this guide
    Definition: Projection of FFF; dependency preservation

    The projection of FFF on RiR_iRi​, πRi(F)\pi_{R_i}(F)πRi​​(F), is the set of FDs X→YX\to YX→Y in F+F^+F+ with X∪Y⊆RiX\cup Y\subseteq R_iX∪Y⊆Ri​. D={R1,…,Rm}D=\{R_1,\dots,R_m\}D={R1​,…,Rm​} is dependency-preserving w.r.t. FFF if

    (πR1(F)∪⋯∪πRm(F))+=F+.\big(\pi_{R_1}(F)\cup\dots\cup\pi_{R_m}(F)\big)^+ = F^+.(πR1​​(F)∪⋯∪πRm​​(F))+=F+.

    The FDs of FFF need not appear literally in some RiR_iRi​; it is enough that they follow from FDs that each lie inside one relation.

    Why it matters. Each FD is an integrity constraint. If it is preserved, the DBMS can enforce it by checking each relation separately on every insert/update (e.g. as a key or UNIQUE constraint). If it is lost, enforcing it requires joining relations after every update, which is impractical, so in practice the constraint goes unenforced and inconsistent data can creep in.

    Practical test (no need to compute projections): for each X→YX\to YX→Y in FFF, set Z:=XZ:=XZ:=X and repeat “for each RiR_iRi​: Z:=Z∪((Z∩Ri)+∩Ri)Z := Z\cup\big((Z\cap R_i)^+\cap R_i\big)Z:=Z∪((Z∩Ri​)+∩Ri​)” until ZZZ stops growing; the FD is preserved iff Y⊆ZY\subseteq ZY⊆Z.

    Example

    LOTS1A(P, C, L, A) = (Property_id, County, Lot#, Area) with F={P→CLA, CL→PA, A→C}F=\{P\to CLA,\ CL\to PA,\ A\to C\}F={P→CLA, CL→PA, A→C}; decompose into LOTS1AX(P,A,L), LOTS1AY(A,C). Projections: on PALPALPAL: P→ALP\to ALP→AL, AL→PAL\to PAL→P (since (AL)+∋P(AL)^+\ni P(AL)+∋P via A→CA\to CA→C, CL→PCL\to PCL→P); on ACACAC: A→CA\to CA→C. Test CL→PCL\to PCL→P: Z=CLZ=CLZ=CL; Z∩PAL=LZ\cap PAL=LZ∩PAL=L, L+=LL^+=LL+=L; Z∩AC=CZ\cap AC=CZ∩AC=C, C+=CC^+=CC+=C; ZZZ never grows, P∉ZP\notin ZP∈/Z. FD2 CL→PACL\to PACL→PA is lost (checked by program). Contrast: the 2NF/3NF splits of LOTS in Fig. 14.12 preserve all FDs.

    Answer

    A decomposition is dependency-preserving if the union of the FDs that hold within the individual relations is equivalent to FFF. It is important because each FD is a constraint: if preserved it can be enforced relation by relation; if lost, it can only be checked by joining relations, which is impractical.

    15.9BCNF vs. dependency preservationE&N Ex. 15.9 · p. 535

    Why can we not guarantee that BCNF relation schemas will be produced by dependency-preserving decompositions of non-BCNF relation schemas? Give a counterexample to illustrate this point.

    Solution · written for this guide

    Why. BCNF forbids every non-trivial FD X→AX\to AX→A whose left side is not a superkey, even when AAA is prime. If AAA is part of a key KKK and X→AX\to AX→A with XXX not a superkey, then BCNF forces XXX and AAA into a separate relation and removes AAA from the rest. But the FD K→…K\to\dotsK→… that needs AAA together with the other key attributes then has no relation containing all its attributes, and cannot be derived from what remains. 3NF tolerates exactly this case (clause: “or AAA is prime”), which is why 3NF with dependency preservation is always achievable (Claim 1) but BCNF is not.

    Counterexample: TEACH(Student, Course, Instructor)

    Write SSS, CCC, III. F={SC→I, I→C}F=\{SC \rightarrow I,\ I \rightarrow C\}F={SC→I, I→C} (an instructor teaches one course).

    • Closures: (SC)+=SCI(SC)^+=SCI(SC)+=SCI, (SI)+=SIC(SI)^+=SIC(SI)+=SIC (via I→CI\to CI→C), I+=ICI^+=ICI+=IC, S+=SS^+=SS+=S, C+=CC^+=CC+=C. Candidate keys SCSCSC and SISISI; all three attributes are prime.
    • 3NF: SC→ISC\to ISC→I has a superkey left side; I→CI\to CI→C has prime right side. In 3NF.
    • BCNF: I→CI\to CI→C with I+=IC≠RI^+=IC\ne RI+=IC=R: III is not a superkey. Not in BCNF.

    Any decomposition into BCNF must be into proper subsets of {S,C,I}\{S,C,I\}{S,C,I}. But SC→ISC\to ISC→I involves all three attributes, so it can lie inside no proper subset, and it cannot be derived from the FDs that do hold inside them: the only non-trivial FDs of F+F^+F+ on two attributes are I→CI\to CI→C (on ICICIC); on SCSCSC and SISISI nothing non-trivial holds. From {I→C}\{I\to C\}{I→C} alone, (SC)+=SC∌I(SC)^+=SC\not\ni I(SC)+=SC∋I. So every proper decomposition loses SC→ISC\to ISC→I (checked by program over all decompositions). The three binary candidates:

    DecompositionNJB: common →\to→ a side?Lossless?Lost FDs
    (S,I),(S,C)(S,I),(S,C)(S,I),(S,C)S+=SS^+=SS+=S: nono (10 spurious tuples on Fig. 14.14 data)SC→ISC\to ISC→I, I→CI\to CI→C
    (C,I),(C,S)(C,I),(C,S)(C,I),(C,S)C+=CC^+=CC+=C: nono (13 spurious tuples)SC→ISC\to ISC→I
    (I,C),(I,S)(I,C),(I,S)(I,C),(I,S)I+∋CI^+\ni CI+∋C: yesyesSC→ISC\to ISC→I

    The best BCNF design is TEACH1(Instructor, Course), TEACH2(Instructor, Student): lossless, both in BCNF, but {Student, Course} →\to→ Instructor is no longer enforceable within one relation (a student could be given two instructors of the same course).

    Answer

    BCNF may force us to split off an FD X→AX\to AX→A with AAA prime, which separates the attributes of a key FD; that FD is then lost. Counterexample: R(S,C,I)R(S,C,I)R(S,C,I), F={SC→I, I→C}F=\{SC\to I,\ I\to C\}F={SC→I, I→C} is in 3NF but not BCNF, and every decomposition into BCNF relations loses SC→ISC\to ISC→I.

    15.10Lossless (nonadditive) joinE&N Ex. 15.10 · p. 535★ Must-do

    What is the lossless (or nonadditive) join property of a decomposition? Why is it important?

    Solution · written for this guide
    Definition: Nonadditive (lossless) join property

    D={R1,…,Rm}D=\{R_1,\dots,R_m\}D={R1​,…,Rm​} of RRR has the lossless join property w.r.t. FFF if for every relation state rrr of RRR that satisfies FFF:

    πR1(r)∗πR2(r)∗⋯∗πRm(r)  =  r.\pi_{R_1}(r) \mathbin{*} \pi_{R_2}(r)\mathbin{*}\dots \mathbin{*}\pi_{R_m}(r) \;=\; r.πR1​​(r)∗πR2​​(r)∗⋯∗πRm​​(r)=r.

    The join always contains rrr; “lossless” means it adds no spurious tuples (“loss” refers to loss of information, which is why the book prefers “nonadditive”).

    Why important. The decomposed relations are what is stored; the original facts are recovered by joining them. If the decomposition is lossy, the join produces tuples that never existed (wrong information), and you cannot tell which are genuine. This property is mandatory (15.11); it must hold for every legal state, so it is tested on the schema and FFF, not on data.

    Tiny illustration

    rrr(Ename, Plocation, Pnumber) ={(Smith,Houston,1), (Wong,Houston,2)}=\{(\text{Smith},\text{Houston},1),\ (\text{Wong},\text{Houston},2)\}={(Smith,Houston,1), (Wong,Houston,2)} split into (Ename, Plocation) and (Plocation, Pnumber): the join on Plocation returns 4 tuples, including the false (Smith, Houston, 2) and (Wong, Houston, 1). Plocation is not a key of either side.

    Test 1: NJB (binary decompositions)

    {R1,R2}\{R_1,R_2\}{R1​,R2​} is lossless iff (R1∩R2)→(R1−R2)(R_1\cap R_2)\to(R_1-R_2)(R1​∩R2​)→(R1​−R2​) or (R1∩R2)→(R2−R1)(R_1\cap R_2)\to(R_2-R_1)(R1​∩R2​)→(R2​−R1​) is in F+F^+F+; i.e. the common attributes are a superkey of one of the two parts. (Reason: if R1∩R2→R2R_1\cap R_2\to R_2R1​∩R2​→R2​, every R1R_1R1​ tuple matches at most one R2R_2R2​ tuple, and that is the one it came from.)

    Test 2: Algorithm 15.3 (chase / tableau; any number of relations)

    Matrix: one row per RiR_iRi​, one column per attribute; row iii has aja_jaj​ in columns of RiR_iRi​, bijb_{ij}bij​ elsewhere. Repeatedly, for each X→YX\to YX→Y in FFF, make rows that agree on XXX agree on YYY (prefer an aaa symbol). Lossless iff some row becomes all aaa. Example (Fig. 15.1): R={R=\{R={Ssn, Ename, Pnumber, Pname, Plocation, Hours}\}}, F={F=\{F={Ssn →\to→ Ename, Pnumber →\to→ {Pname, Plocation}, {Ssn, Pnumber} →\to→ Hours}\}}.

    (a) D={R1,R2}D=\{R_1, R_2\}D={R1​,R2​} with R1=R_1=R1​= EMP_LOCS(Ename, Plocation) and R2=R_2=R2​= EMP_PROJ1(Ssn, Pnumber, Hours, Pname, Plocation):

    SsnEnamePnumberPnamePlocationHours
